data.title: The secret to financial happiness - and it’s not the size of your paycheck
data.ai_summary: A Klarna study found that understanding finances is more strongly linked to life satisfaction than income alone, with covering unexpected bills twice as impactful. Participants who knew their money better felt more in control and made fewer budgeting mistakes. The research suggests financial clarity can boost wellbeing and mental health.
data.author: Sarah Ingram

company_mentions.name: London School of Economics and Political Science

data.full_text:
The secret to financial happiness - and it’s not the size of your paycheck Share Article Add us as preferred source By Sarah Ingram

Professor Paul Dolan of the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)

Money can’t buy you happiness but knowing just how much you’ve got can certainly help. New research has revealed that understanding your finances can be as important to wellbeing as a big paycheck - and could even make holidays more enjoyable. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT The study by Klarna found that predictable income was more strongly associated with life satisfaction than earnings alone and being able to cover an unexpected bill was around twice as strongly linked to life satisfaction as income. Published today as The Clarity Effect, the research was carried out by leading behavioural scientists and explores how financial understanding affects happiness. Subscribe Invalid email You agree you are 18 or over. We use your sign-up to provide content in ways you've consented to and to improve our understanding of you. This may include adverts from us and third parties based on our knowledge of you. You can unsubscribe at any time. More Info. Participants took part in a series of experiments where their finances remained the same but the information available to them changed. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Despite having identical circumstances, people who knew more about their money looked forward to future plans more, felt more in control and made fewer budgeting mistakes. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT In one experiment, people given a budgeting tool while planning a holiday felt more excited about their trip and imagined it more vividly. When subsequently asked to picture their holiday, those without the tool were almost four times as likely to think about money (11% versus 3%). In another experiment, people awaiting a car repair bill felt more in control when told it would cost £200 rather than somewhere between £100 and £300 - despite the expected cost being identical. Together, the findings suggest that happiness may depend not just on how much money we have, but on how clearly we understand and manage it. The research was carried out by Professor Paul Dolan of the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), supported by Professor Micael Dahlen of the Stockholm School of Economics. “We tend to assume that people who keep track of their money are missing out on fun. Our research suggests the opposite: when you’re on top of your finances, your mind is free to wander to fun places, including future experiences,” he said. “Knowing where you stand isn’t boring, it’s what helps you free up headspace and boost wellbeing.” The research suggests that using budgeting tools to help you understand and manage finances may come with additional benefits for mental health. Magnus Lindholm, head of consumer marketing at Klarna, added: “Financial tools should give people the clarity and confidence to make informed decisions, without money becoming a constant distraction. Like a good football referee, they should work in the background, stepping in when needed to keep things running smoothly.” The research was carried out in collaboration with Headspace. Dr Jenna Glover, chief clinical officer for the mental health and mindfulness platform added: “People often assume that earning more reduces stress, but psychologically what calms us is a sense of control. “Financial clarity eases the mental load, giving you both the confidence you can cover the unexpected and the headspace to enjoy life to the fullest.” How to reduce the money mental load Keep everything in one place: Having income and bills organised in a single view helped people feel clearer about their finances. Keep a running total: Tracking spending against a budget reduced the risk of overspending and helped people look forward to future plans. Confirm costs upfront: Knowing the exact amount of a bill helped people feel more in control. Ask for fixed quotes and confirm costs early wherever possible. Stay informed, but don't over-check: While knowing where you stand can improve wellbeing, frequently checking your balance was linked to greater worry rather than happiness.

data.title: Acquirers Are Snapping Up Boom-Era Startups That Haven’t Raised Funding In Years
data.ai_summary: Uber acquired ezCater for $2.3 billion, nearly five years after its last funding round. Other deals include Miro, Airtable, and Headspace, all at valuations far below their peaks. The analysis shows acquirers are buying well-funded startups that haven't raised equity in four or more years.
data.author: Joanna Glasner

industries.name: Corporate M&A / Venture Build-to-Buy Programs (Acqui-hire, option-to-acquire)

data.full_text:
0 Shares Email

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn When a venture-backed startup goes a few years without raising a new round, it’s common to presume its odds of a sizable exit have gone down as well. But that’s often not the case, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. This year, a number of larger acquisitions of private companies involved startups that haven’t disclosed a new investment for more than four years. Several of these acquisitions are quite recent — and in some cases, quite large. The standout is Uber’s purchase earlier this month of ezCater, a platform for catering and workplace meals, for $2.3 billion in cash. The deal comes nearly five years after Boston-based ezCater raised its last reported venture funding round. That’s not the only one. A number of companies whose names might feature on a playlist of 2021 boom-era unicorns have sold to acquirers in recent months, including one-time highfliers like Airtable, Headspace and Miro. In many cases, companies are selling at valuations which, while not puny, are still far below their former peaks. Who’s getting acquired To illustrate the extent to which these aging startups are finding acquirers, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of 15 deals involving well-funded companies that haven’t raised equity funding for four or more years. Post-peak runway One big issue for older and middle-aged startups is that valuations hit a cyclical peak in 2021 and early 2022. Many companies that raised during that time had difficulty attracting fresh capital or were reluctant to close new rounds at reduced valuations. Even with the more recent AI boom, little went to this cohort. Moreover, since the 2021 boom-era rounds were quite large, funded startups commonly had the option to cut operating costs and extend their runways with existing capital. As a result, quite a few companies that haven’t raised rounds in years are still chugging along, managing to survive and even grow without more venture funding. EzCater is a case in point. In the year prior to its acquisition, the business generated more than $2.5 billion in gross bookings. It had an annual growth rate in the high teens, with average order sizes over $400. That said, even that revenue and growth rate didn’t secure ezCater much of an acquisition premium from its last funding round. At $2.3 billion, Uber’s purchase price is 53% above the $1.5 billion pre-money valuation the catering startup secured in its last funding round in late 2021. Acquisitions below peak venture valuation In many cases, even good-sized acquisitions of well-funded startups are occurring at valuations far below former peaks. Take Miro, a provider of online collaboration tools that agreed to sell to Bending Spoons last month in a deal valued around $1.36 billion. That’s a huge step down from early 2022, when San Francisco-based Miro closed its last round at a $17.5 billion post-money valuation. Or consider Bending Spoons’ prior purchase of data and workflow platform Airtable, for $1.28 billion in August. That’s barely over one-tenth the $11 billion valuation Airtable secured in its December 2021 Series F. Fashion startup Everlane is another that lost its shimmer after securing a 2020 valuation in the hundreds of millions. It sold to fast-fashion leader Shein this spring for $100 million. In the health and wellness sector, meanwhile, Headspace also saw its valuation plunge. The meditation and mental health app sold to Sword Health in a deal reportedly valued around $300 million. That’s well below its peak post-money valuation of around $2.6 billion. A good thing? While startup investors aren’t celebrating acquisitions made far under peak private valuations, they’re not the worst outcome. And for startups themselves, they’re also far from a catastrophic scenario. Of course, every unicorn investor hopes for high-multiple returns. But for startups that go years without funding, the market seems to be telling us that’s not likely in the cards. Related Crunchbase list: Acquired Startups That Hadn’t Raised Venture Funding For 4+ Years

data.title: Brellium Raises $23 Million And Launches CortexLM For AI-Powered Clinical Compliance
data.ai_summary: Brellium raised $23 million in venture funding led by Left Lane Capital and First Round Capital, and launched CortexLM, an AI system that analyzes patient notes for clinical compliance and billing issues. The company has audited about 22 million visits and protected nearly $2 billion in revenue, supporting over 215,000 providers. It plans to expand into cardiology, pain management, and primary care.
data.author: Amit Chowdhry

industries.name: Clinical Coding Support (ICD/CPT/SNOMED) & Documentation Compliance Tools

data.full_text: Brellium has raised $23 million in venture funding and launched CortexLM, a proprietary AI system designed to analyze patient notes for gaps in clinical care, documentation, billing compliance, and revenue integrity. The financing was led by Left Lane Capital and First Round Capital, with participation from Digital Health Venture Partners. Brellium plans to use the capital to expand into additional medical specialties, serve more provider organizations, and move deeper into the healthcare revenue cycle. CortexLM analyzes patient documentation before billing and can flag potential errors while proposing corrections. Brellium said the system is trained around the requirements relevant to individual providers, creating what the company describes as an audit-ready record designed to reduce exposure to denials, recoupments, and compliance issues. The company has audited approximately 22 million patient visits and said its technology has protected nearly $2 billion in provider revenue from potential recoupments. Brellium currently supports more than 215,000 healthcare providers and approximately 200 provider groups across all 50 states. Customers include Gentiva, Maxim Healthcare, Rula, and Headspace. Headspace expanded its clinical quality assurance program from reviewing approximately 2% of therapy notes to 100% after implementing Brellium. The company said Headspace subsequently achieved 99.2% provider compliance with documentation standards. Brellium also offers a financial guarantee under which it says it will cover certain costs if CMS or a payer later identifies an issue in documentation that Brellium previously cleared. The funding will help Brellium broaden its reach into high-stakes specialties including cardiology, pain management, and primary care. Its broader platform is positioned around clinical compliance and revenue integrity, with AI analyzing documentation and coding before problems turn into payer clawbacks or missed reimbursement. KEY QUOTES: “Providers and payers have been stuck fighting the same fraud, waste and abuse problem from opposite sides of the table for years. CortexLM is how we get everyone working from the same standard, so providers can prove the care was right the first time, instead of spending months untangling it after the fact.” Zach Rosen, Co-Founder And CEO Of Brellium “We were excited to double down and back Brellium again because of their exceptional execution since first starting to work with them. The team is laser-focused on creating a product that adds real value for their customers.” Henry Toole, Partner At Left Lane Capital “The biggest benefit of Brellium is peace of mind in ensuring high-quality patient care.” Jon Kole, Medical Director At Headspace Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. data.title: [IT 핸즈온] 생활습관 바꾼 손가락 위 주치의 '오우라링5'
data.ai_summary: A two-month review of Oura Ring 5, a smart ring, found it changed health habits by tracking sleep, activity, and stress. The ring's data matched self-perceived fatigue, and push notifications prompted movement. However, the 630,000-780,000 won price and 9,400 won monthly subscription are burdensome.
data.author: 블로터; 네이버

industries.name: Mental Wellness & Stress Management Devices (Biofeedback, Meditation/Neurostimulation Devices)

data.full_text:
손가락에 낀 은색 반지 하나에 주변의 관심이 쏟아졌다. 별다른 장식도, 반짝이는 보석도 없다. 언뜻 보면 평범한 패션 반지지만 정체는 조금 특별하다. 심박수와 체온은 물론 수면과 신체 회복 상태까지 살펴보는 스마트링이다. 핀란드 웨어러블 기기 업체 오우라(Oura)가 8월 출시한 최신 제품 '오우라링5'다. 17일 기준 약 두 달간 직접 착용해 보니 단순히 건강 수치를 기록하는 기기를 넘어 생활 습관까지 바꾸게 만드는 건강관리 도구에 가까웠다.
자는 동안 수면 분석, 깨어 있을 땐 활동·스트레스 관리
처음 제품을 손에 쥐었을 때 가장 놀라웠던 점은 무게다. 플라스틱인가 싶을 정도로 가벼웠다. 하지만 실제 소재는 티타늄이다. 직접 착용한 제품은 은색 표면에 미세한 결을 살린 '브러시드 실버(Brushed Silver)' 색상이다. 스마트워치처럼 화면이나 버튼도 없어 겉모습만으로 전자기기라는 사실을 알아채기 어렵다.반지 바깥쪽에는 작은 타원형 표시가 있다. 단순한 장식처럼 보이는 무늬지만 착용 방향을 확인하는 역할을 한다. 표시가 손바닥 쪽을 향하도록 끼우면 안쪽 센서가 손가락에 밀착한다. 전작보다 부피를 40% 줄이고 두께를 2.28㎜로 낮췄다. 실제 손가락에 낀 채 잠들어도 이물감이 없었다. 자는 동안 반지를 착용하고 있다는 사실조차 잊을 정도였다.
처음에는 작은 반지 하나가 건강 상태에 대해 얼마나 많은 정보를 알려줄 수 있을지 의문이었다. 그러나 두 달간 사용하면서 가장 크게 달라진 것은 스스로 몸을 바라보는 방식이었다. 평소에는 몇 시간을 잤는지조차 별다른 관심이 없었다. 전날 늦게 잠들어 피곤하면 단순히 잠이 부족한 탓이라고 생각하는 정도였다.
오우라링5를 착용하면서 달라졌다. 아침에 일어나면 스마트폰의 오우라 애플리케이션(앱)을 열어 전날 수면 점수와 신체 회복 상태부터 확인하게 됐다. 수면 시간뿐 아니라 깊은 수면과 얕은 수면, 렘(REM)수면 등 수면 단계별 시간과 수면 효율까지 살펴볼 수 있었다.
특히 흥미로웠던 것은 측정 결과가 실제 몸 상태와 상당 부분 일치했다는 점이다. 아침부터 유난히 피곤했던 날에는 수면이나 회복 관련 지표도 좋지 않았다. 반대로 비교적 개운하게 일어난 날에는 측정 결과도 긍정적이었다. 평소에는 단순히 '오늘 좀 피곤하네' 하고 넘겼을 몸 상태를 숫자로 확인할 수 있었다.과식하거나 술을 마신 날에는 차이가 더욱 눈에 띄었다. 평소보다 많이 먹거나 음주한 뒤 잠자리에 들면 다음 날 수면의 질이 낮아진 결과를 확인할 수 있었다. 몸이 무겁고 피곤하다고 느낀 날에는 데이터도 비슷한 방향을 가리켰다. 매일 아침 수면 점수를 확인하다 보니 언제 잠들었고 얼마나 깊이 잤는지 자연스럽게 돌아보게 됐다. 점수를 조금이라도 개선하고 싶다는 생각에 가능한 한 비슷한 시간에 잠자리에 들려고 노력하기 시작했다.
생활 습관을 바꾸는 데는 수면 점수뿐 아니라 낮 시간에 도착하는 푸시 알림도 한몫했다. 한창 업무에 집중하던 오후3시20분에 "잠깐 다리를 쭉 펴 볼까요?"라는 알림이 도착했다. 앞서 오후2시20분에는 "14분 빠르게 걸으면 목표를 달성할 수 있어요. 할 수 있어요!"라는 응원 섞인 메시지가 떴다.
평소 컴퓨터 앞에 앉아 업무를 보다 보면 얼마나 오랫동안 움직이지 않았는지 의식하지 못할 때가 많다. 하지만 스마트폰에 나타나는 짧은 메시지를 보면 잠깐 자리에서 일어나거나 걸어야겠다는 생각이 들었다. 건강 상태를 측정하는 데서 그치지 않고 생활 속 작은 실천을 유도한다는 점이 인상적이었다. 심박수와 심박변이도, 체온 등의 생체 데이터를 분석해 낮 동안 신체가 받는 스트레스 수준과 회복 상태도 보여준다. 스트레스가 높아지는 시간대와 회복 추이를 확인할 수 있어 업무 중 언제 몸에 부담이 커지는지 살펴보고 휴식을 취하는 데도 도움이 됐다.
쌓일수록 정교해지는 건강 데이터…맞춤형 코칭까지, 구독료는 부담
오우라링의 진가는 사용 기간이 길어질수록 드러난다. 처음에는 하루하루의 건강 지표를 확인하는 데 집중했지만 시간이 지나면서 수면의 질과 신체 회복 상태, 심박수, 스트레스 수준 등 다양한 생체 지표가 어떻게 변화하는지 살펴볼 수 있어 유용했다. 오우라 앱은 주간·월간·분기별·연간 보고서를 제공한다. 수면·준비 상태·활동 점수와 안정 시 심박수, 심박변이도 등의 변화 추이를 확인할 수 있다. 매일 기록한 데이터가 쌓이면서 자신의 건강 상태를 중장기적으로 살펴볼 수 있는 건강 일지가 만들어지는 셈이다.수면 습관을 장기적으로 관리하는 데 도움이 되는 기능은 '크로노타입(Chronotype)'이다. 오우라는 수면과 활동량, 체온 등 장기간 축적한 데이터를 바탕으로 사용자의 생체리듬을 이른 아침형부터 늦은 저녁형까지 6가지 유형으로 구분한다. '체내 시계(Body Clock)'에서는 실제 수면 시간대와 생체리듬에 적합한 시간대를 비교해 개인의 몸에 맞는 수면 습관을 찾도록 돕는다.
여성 건강 기능도 장기간 축적한 생체 데이터를 활용하는 대표적인 사례다. '생리 주기 인사이트(Cycle Insights)'는 체온 변화와 생리 기록 등을 활용해 월경 주기를 추적하고 다음 생리 시작일을 예측한다. 임신 주수에 따른 신체 변화를 살펴보거나 폐경이행기 증상을 기록하는 기능도 제공한다. 단순히 수면이나 운동량을 측정하는 데 그치지 않고 여성의 생애주기 전반으로 건강관리 영역을 확대한 것이다.
최근 공개한 '헬스 레이더(Health Radar)' 역시 장기간 축적한 데이터를 활용하는 기능이다. 심혈관과 호흡 관련 생체 신호, 신체 부담 징후 등을 종합적으로 분석해 평소와 다른 건강 패턴을 포착하도록 설계했다. 개인마다 평소 심박수나 호흡 패턴이 다른 만큼 장기간 축적한 데이터를 기준으로 변화를 살핀다.
축적한 개인 데이터를 바탕으로 건강관리의 방향도 제시한다. 단순히 수면이나 활동량을 측정하고 점수를 매기는 데 그치지 않고, 사용자가 일상에서 건강을 개선하기 위해 실천할 수 있는 방법까지 안내한다. 앱의 '둘러보기' 메뉴를 열면 명상과 호흡, 수면, 학습 등 4가지 항목의 콘텐츠가 나타난다.여기에는 불안한 순간을 관리하는 7분 과정과 스트레스·수면을 다루는 15분 과정, 활력 회복을 위한 27분 과정 등이 마련돼 있다. 명상·호흡 전문 서비스 헤드스페이스(Headspace)가 제공하는 콘텐츠도 포함됐다. 일부 프로그램에서는 이용 전후 심박수와 심박변이도 변화를 확인할 수도 있다. 자신의 건강 상태를 파악하는 데서 나아가 개선을 위한 실천 방법까지 안내하고 신체 반응도 확인할 수 있다는 점에서 단순한 건강 측정 기기보다 개인의 일상을 관리해주는 맞춤형 건강 코치에 가깝게 느껴졌다.
가격은 아쉬운 부분이다. 국내 출시가격은 실버·블랙이 63만원, 골드·스텔스·브러시드 실버·딥 로즈가 78만원이다. 제품 가격 못지않게 부담스러운 것은 구독료다. 주요 건강 분석 기능을 계속 이용하려면 월 9400원의 유료 멤버십에도 가입해야 한다. 월 구독료가 크지 않아 보일 수 있지만 1년이면 11만2800원, 3년이면 33만8400원에 달한다. 특히 장기간 건강 데이터를 축적하고 분석하는 것이 제품의 핵심 가치인 만큼 구독을 중단하기도 쉽지 않다. 이미 60만~80만원에 달하는 비용을 지불하고도 핵심 기능을 이용하기 위해 매달 추가 비용을 내야 한다는 점은 부담이다.
손가락에 낀 반지가 실제 의사를 대신할 수는 없다. 하지만 잠자는 동안부터 깨어 있는 시간까지 몸 상태를 살피고 생활 습관을 바꾸도록 돕는다는 점에서는 '손가락 위 작은 주치의'라는 표현이 어색하지 않았다. 약 두 달간 사용하면서 가장 만족스러웠던 점은 평소 무심하게 지나쳤던 건강에 자연스럽게 관심을 갖게 된 점이다. 자신의 건강 상태를 꾸준히 점검하고 생활 습관을 개선하고 싶은 사람이라면 적극 추천할 만한 제품이다. 높은 가격과 구독료 부담에도 매일 건강을 챙기는 습관을 만들어준다는 점에서 충분한 매력을 느꼈다.

data.title: Headspace Issues Layoffs Following Sword Health Acquisition
data.ai_summary: Sword Health began post-acquisition layoffs after its $300 million purchase of Headspace closed. The combined U.S. workforce was 1,203 before cuts, with planned reductions to create efficiencies. The deal aims to support Sword's future IPO, potentially by 2028.
data.author: Ashleigh Hollowell

industries.name: M&A HR Advisory (Due Diligence, Integration, Carve-outs)

data.full_text:
It has been a little over two weeks since Sword Health’s acquisition of the San Francisco-based digital therapy and psychiatry company Headspace officialy closed and now the combined entity has started to roll out post-transaction layoffs.
Public documents filed by Sword Health and Headspace part of the transaction show that Sword Health employed 624 people in the U.S. before the acquisition. The deal would have added 579 Headspace employees nationwide, bringing the combined U.S. workforce to 1,203 before layoffs.
These documents also note that the post-transaction layoffs were planned.
“Sword anticipates reducing its corporate staff to create efficiencies where redundancies exist between the two organizations after being combined,” one document states.
While neither Headspace nor Sword Health would share details with Behavioral Health Business about the scope or scale of the post-acquisition layoffs, a collection of social media posts suggests that several have been made at director and senior levels, as well as in other roles.
However, it appears that Headspace’s C-suite team including CEO Tom Pickett, Karan Singh the chief operating officer, Dr. Jenna Glover the chief clinical officer and Lisa Mulrooney Gross the chief people officer, have all retained their leadership roles at this time.
Neither company wished to comment on this story, but both were contacted.
The transaction, reportedly valued at $300 million, was a major move by Sword Health to expand further into the behavioral health space. Prior to June 2025, the New York City-based digital health provider mainly offered digital physical therapy programs focused on pain management and prevention. But it entered the mental health space with the launch of an AI tool called Mind after reaching a $1 billion valuation.
Adding Headspace’s network of clients, clinicians and payer relationships marked a major consolidation of digital mental health organizations. A pattern that was also noticeable throughout the broader market earlier in 2026, among other transactions as well.
Moving into behavioral health was also part of Sword Health CEO Virgilio Bento’s goal to inch closer to an official IPO in the future, which he previously told BHB, could become reality by 2028.
In the past, Headspace’s former CEO hinted at eyeing its own IPO. Those separate IPO goals have now become infused as Headspace became part of Sword. Though it remains to be seen whether this transaction will speed up that IPO timeline or not.
Sword Health did not comment on whether additional layoffs might be planned as the Headspace integration continues.

data.title: This ‘CoComelon’ Bedtime Podcast Could Make Nights Easier for Tired Parents
data.ai_summary: CoComelon launched the Wiggle to Wind Down podcast with Headspace, featuring host Dora Kamau and pediatrician Jon Kole. The 20-minute episodes use a three-step routine—wiggling, stretching, breathing—plus a Sleepy Star reward and a bedtime story. The podcast aims to provide a consistent, screen-free bedtime routine for tired parents.
data.author: Elisabeth Sherman

industries.name: Infant & Toddler Sleep, Feeding & Diapering Support Programs

data.full_text:
This ‘CoComelon’ Bedtime Podcast Could Make Nights Easier for Tired Parents
Here’s how ‘Wiggle to Wind Down’ helps parents create a reliable bedtime routine for their toddlers.
Key Takeaways
The 'Wiggle to Wind Down' podcast helps kids release energy, relax their bodies, and settle their minds for sleep with a simple three-step routine.
Each episode is short, consistent, and easy to fit into busy evenings, making bedtime less stressful for parents.
The podcast encourages screen-free bonding, giving parents and kids a calm, shared moment before bed.
CoComelon has earned a reputation for having parents' backs during some of their toughest parenting moments. Teaching your kids good table manners? CoComelon has a playlist of songs for that. Having trouble potty training your toddler? You can bet CoComelon's potty training resources won't let you down.
So, it makes sense that the toddler entertainment franchise would delve into the sometimes nightmarish world of child sleep, with a newly launched podcast called Wiggle to Wind Down.
The 'CoComelon' Podcast Was Designed for Better Sleep
I say nightmarish because every parent, at one time or another, has bribed, begged, or pleaded with their little one to go to bed, and, ideally, stay there. To help parents on their quest for a goodnight's rest (and make bedtime less of a battle), CoComelon teamed up with Headspace to produce the podcast, and recruited meditation teacher Dora Kamau as the host.
The team at CoComelon consulted with Jon Kole, MD, pediatrician and child psychiatrist, to make sure the sleep advice they're offering kids is expert-vetted.
"What sets this podcast apart is its structure, which is scientifically grounded in the principles of regulation, rest, and sleep in early childhood, and delivered in a consistent, appealing format," Dr. Kole tells Parents.
The 20-minute podcast has a "three-step structure," Dr. Kole explains. First, as the title suggests, kids wiggle around to release energy. Then, they stretch to bring "ease and physical awareness" to their bodies. Finally, they are instructed to do some basic breathing exercises, which "signal to the body and mind that it's time to settle."
The Podcast Rewards Following Routine
There's also what Dr. Kole calls a "behavioral cue." After completing each of the three steps, the kids listening receive a Sleepy Star—positive reinforcement that encourages kids to stick to the routine laid out by the podcast. After all, as Dr. Kole reminds us, "consistency is what trains the child's brain for sleep."
The Sleepy Star is at least, in theory, supposed to switch up how kids think about bedtime. Dr. Kole says that when you cajole and pester your child about bedtime, they are in a "compliance" mindset—and what toddler doesn't resist complying with what their parents ask them to do?
The reward of the star, on the other hand, is supposed to make them think about going to sleep like an "achievement, which encourages participation and control."
The Podcast Lets Listeners 'Wind Down' With a Story
Following the three-step routine, the podcast transitions into a bedtime story. As any sleep expert will tell you, the key to a good night's rest is a predictable routine.
So while the bedtime story changes, the main component of the podcast does not. Parents and kids will encounter wiggling, stretching, and breathing exercises in each episode, giving your child that consistent routine their bodies need to sleep well, night after night.
Dr. Kole calls the podcast a "predictable, evidence-based roadmap for regulating their child's energy and emotions."
Busy Families Benefit From the Podcast's Simple Structure
Headspace designed the podcast to accommodate even the busiest families, who are already carrying a heavy mental load. Parents are already scheduling play dates and doctor's appointments, so mapping out a bedtime routine can feel insurmountable. The podcast is meant to do some of the bedtime planning for parents, taking an intimidating task off their plate.
"The fatigue of deciding what to do is often more draining than the action itself," Dr. Kole says. But the Wiggle to Wind Down podcast is a "complete routine in a single brief audio package."
Dr. Kole adds, "The total runtime of each episode is purposefully concise. This duration is the sweet spot that is long enough to be effective, but short enough to be realistic for a tired parent's schedule."
The consistent length and structure of each episode allows parents to easily integrate the podcast into their evenings. "Right after the final essentials, like pajamas, brushing their teeth, and right before 'lights out,'" says Dr. Kole.
It Helps Families Bond, Too
The format also allows for an opportunity for screen-free bonding with your child (most pediatric experts agree that screens should be turned off one hour before bedtime anyway). Parents who work full time, or have a backlog of chores and other errands on their minds, might have trouble being present with their children in the evenings.
But while Wiggle to Wind Down is technically intended for kids, Dr. Kole thinks the podcast offers both parents and kids a chance to focus on each other. Instead of scrolling on your phone, you can go through each step of the routine together, says Dr. Kole, giving your toddler "undivided, calm attention."
"This shared moment of presence is the most important," he continues, "and often most missed, component of a successful bedtime routine in a busy home."

data.title: Brellium Raises $23M and Launches CortexLM with a Financial Guarantee Against Payer Clawbacks
data.ai_summary: Brellium raised $23M in venture financing and launched CortexLM, a machine-learning platform that audits 100% of patient notes before billing. The company has audited over 22 million visits, protecting nearly $2 billion in revenue, and offers a financial guarantee against payer clawbacks. The funds will expand into high-complexity specialties and deepen billing integrations.
data.author: Fred Pennic
data.full_text:
Brellium Raises $23M and Launches CortexLM with a Financial Guarantee Against Payer Clawbacks

What You Should Know Healthcare clinical compliance and revenue integrity platform Brellium raises $23M in venture financing, co-led by Left Lane Capital and First Round Capital, with participation from Digital Health Venture Partners (and prior backing from Menlo Ventures).

Directly tackles the escalating “healthcare bot war” over claims adjudication and post-payment clawbacks, positioning itself as a shared, objective standard between healthcare providers and health insurance payers rather than fueling unilateral AI-to-AI disputes.

Unveiled CortexLM, Brellium’s proprietary machine-learning architecture engineered to review and audit 100% of patient notes before billing, flagging care gaps, coding inconsistencies, and compliance errors, and proposing specific documentation remediations calibrated to specialty, payer, and regulatory guidelines. Technical Architecture: CortexLM and Pre-Bill Chart Correction CortexLM transitions clinical chart auditing from retrospective damage control to proactive, pre-submission revenue integrity. Rather than relying on random statistical spot-checks, CortexLM reads and analyzes 100% of individual patient notes across a practice. The model evaluates chart documentation against specialty-specific clinical practice parameters, individual commercial payer medical policies, CMS billing regulations, and quality reporting criteria. By operating prior to billing, the system identifies diagnostic inconsistencies, missing documentation components, coding gaps, and non-compliant phrasing before claims are submitted to clearinghouses or payers. CortexLM then proposes specific clinical documentation fixes to treating providers while encounters are fresh. In addition to mitigating clawback exposure, the system audits for legitimate clinical complexity and documentation integrity, uncovering billable services and comorbidities that providers delivered but omitted from final claim drops. Brellium has achieved national enterprise penetration across multi-specialty medical groups, home health systems, and high-volume behavioral health networks. The platform is currently trusted by more than 215,000 clinicians across 200 provider groups operating in all 50 U.S. states. To date, Brellium has processed and audited more than 22 million patient visits, protecting nearly $2 billion in provider revenue from post-payment recoupments, payer clawbacks, and audit penalties. Enterprise customers include national home health and post-acute providers Gentiva and Maxim Healthcare, as well as scaled behavioral health networks Headspace and Rula. At Headspace, adopting Brellium enabled the organization to scale its clinical quality assurance coverage from auditing two percent of therapy notes to 100%, driving provider compliance with clinical documentation standards to 99.2%. The Brellium Audit Guarantee The defining commercial innovation of Brellium’s model is its financial guarantee. If CMS, a Medicare Administrative Contractor, or a private commercial health plan audits a chart and issues a financial clawback or penalty on a visit that Brellium previously reviewed and cleared, Brellium foots the bill instead of the provider. This structure directly tackles the primary liability barrier identified in the Bessemer and Bain 2026 Healthcare AI ROI Scorecard, which noted that clinicians and provider organizations routinely avoid scaling AI because they bear full medico-legal and financial liability for algorithmic outputs. By putting its own balance sheet behind its algorithmic auditing engine, Brellium removes the liability defense used by risk-averse CFOs and compliance committees, elevating its software from a passive documentation tool to an insurable standard of truth. Expansion Roadmap: Deepening Revenue Cycle and High-Stakes Specialties The $23M capital raise will be deployed to broaden clinical coverage and deepen billing integration. Brellium is scaling beyond its foundational footprint in behavioral health and home care into high-complexity, high-dollar specialties heavily targeted by Recovery Audit Contractors, including cardiology, interventional pain management, and value-based primary care. Operationally, the company is deepening bi-directional integrations with practice management and EHR billing engines to automate coding validation, modifier application, and pre-claim clearinghouse handoffs. Brellium is also expanding conversations with health plans to position CortexLM as a shared, objective pre-payment validation layer, enabling auto-adjudication and clean-claim passes that eliminate post-payment audit friction entirely. “Providers and payers have been stuck fighting the same fraud, waste and abuse problem from opposite sides of the table for years,” said Zach Rosen, Co-Founder and CEO of Brellium. “CortexLM is how we get everyone working from the same standard, so providers can prove the care was right the first time, instead of spending months untangling it after the fact.”

data.title: Brellium raises $23M to catch medical billing errors with AI and protect healthcare providers from costly audits
data.ai_summary: Brellium raised $23 million in venture funding to expand its AI billing-error detection platform, CortexLM. The system has audited over 22 million patient visits and helped protect nearly $2 billion in provider revenue. The company plans to extend its technology into cardiology, pain management, and primary care.
data.author: Daniel Levi
data.full_text:
0 Shares

New York-based healthcare AI startup Brellium has raised $23 million in venture funding to help healthcare providers catch medical billing errors, identify gaps in patient care, and avoid costly insurance audits before problems become financial losses. The company announced the funding alongside the launch of CortexLM, an AI system that reviews patient records for documentation errors and compliance risks before claims reach insurers. The round was led by Left Lane Capital and First Round Capital, with participation from Digital Health Venture Partners. Brellium plans to use the capital to reach more healthcare organizations and extend its technology into additional medical specialties. The funding announcement comes as healthcare providers face growing scrutiny over billing practices from government agencies and private insurers. A missing detail in a patient’s medical record or an incorrect billing code can trigger a denied insurance claim, repayment demand, or regulatory investigation. For large healthcare organizations processing millions of visits, those mistakes can add up quickly. Brellium wants to catch those problems before they become expensive. Its new CortexLM system uses AI to examine clinical notes, compare them against insurance and regulatory requirements, and flag potential errors. Rather than reviewing a small sample of patient records, the software checks every clinical note and recommends corrections before billing. The company says its platform has already audited more than 22 million patient visits and helped protect nearly $2 billion in healthcare provider revenue from potential repayment demands. Those figures are company-reported. Brellium wants to catch healthcare billing mistakes before insurers do Founded in 2021, Brellium is building software that addresses one of healthcare’s less visible but financially significant problems: ensuring medical records accurately reflect the care patients receive and meet the requirements insurers use to approve payments. Traditional medical chart reviews often rely on staff to manually examine only a fraction of patient records. Brellium’s approach replaces that sampling process with automated reviews across an organization’s entire patient population. CortexLM takes that approach further by checking documentation against the requirements of individual providers, insurers, and clinical programs. It can flag missing information, incorrect billing codes, and potential care quality issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. “Providers and payers have been stuck fighting the same fraud, waste, and abuse problem from opposite sides of the table for years,” said Zach Rosen, co-founder and CEO of Brellium. “CortexLM is how we get everyone working from the same standard, so providers can prove the care was right the first time, instead of spending months untangling it after the fact.” The company points to mental healthcare provider Headspace as an example of the technology in practice. Before adopting Brellium, Headspace reviewed roughly 2% of its therapy notes through its clinical quality assurance program. After implementing the software, the organization increased that figure to 100%, according to Brellium. The company says Headspace now reports 99.2% compliance with its documentation standards. “The biggest benefit of Brellium is peace of mind in ensuring high-quality patient care,” said Jon Kole, Headspace’s medical director. Brellium is taking an unusual approach to winning customer trust. The company says it will cover repayment costs if an insurer or the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services identifies a qualifying problem in a medical record that its software previously cleared. The announcement did not detail the limits or conditions of that guarantee. Brellium reports serving more than 215,000 healthcare providers across 200 provider groups in all 50 states. Its customers include Gentiva, Maxim Healthcare, Rula, and Headspace. The latest investment will support its move into cardiology, pain management, and primary care, where billing requirements and clinical documentation can be particularly demanding. Brellium previously raised $16.7 million in Series A funding in April 2025, backed by First Round Capital, Left Lane Capital, and other investors. The bigger opportunity goes beyond catching billing mistakes. Healthcare organizations lose time and money correcting rejected claims, responding to audits, and reviewing patient records. Brellium is betting that AI can shift that work to the beginning of the billing process, helping providers address potential problems before insurers find them. The challenge will be proving that automated reviews consistently catch meaningful errors without creating new ones. For healthcare providers, the value of AI-driven compliance software will depend on its accuracy, the work it saves, and the financial losses it actually prevents. 0 Shares

data.full_text:
Brellium, an AI-powered clinical compliance and revenue integrity platform, has raised US$23 million in venture funding and introduced CortexLM, a proprietary system designed to audit patient notes for care and compliance gaps. The round was led by Left Lane Capital and First Round Capital, with participation from Digital Health Venture Partners. The company reports that its technology already protects nearly US$2 billion in provider revenue across more than 22 million patient visits.
Responding to Heightened Audit Pressure
Federal and private payers have sharply increased scrutiny of healthcare billing, forcing providers to defend every dollar and patient note against varied payer, regulatory, and quality rules. By the time issues surface, they often appear as denials, clawbacks, or care errors rather than preventable gaps. Brellium positions CortexLM as a way to align providers and payers around a single standard before claims are challenged.
How CortexLM Works
CortexLM acts as a chart-auditing system that reads every patient note, catches errors, and proposes fixes in care and clinical documentation before billing occurs. The system is trained against each provider organization's specific requirements, creating a defensible and audit-ready record that protects revenue while adding a layer of quality assurance. Brellium has audited 22 million patient visits to date and reports that it has protected nearly US$2 billion in provider revenue from recoupments.
Investor Confidence and Market Need
Left Lane Capital partner Henry Toole said the firm was excited to double down on Brellium because of the team's exceptional execution since its initial work with the company. He added that while compliance is not the most glamorous part of the market, the platform is the infrastructure everything else depends on. CEO Zach Rosen emphasized that providers and payers have been stuck fighting fraud, waste, and abuse from opposite sides for years, and CortexLM can establish a common standard.
Customer Outcomes
Headspace scaled its clinical quality assurance program from reviewing 2% of therapy notes to 100% after adopting Brellium, and it now reports 99.2% provider compliance with documentation standards. Brellium also offers a guarantee that if CMS or a payer finds a problem after the platform has cleared it, Brellium will pay instead of the provider. Jon Kole, medical director at Headspace, said the biggest benefit is peace of mind in ensuring high-quality patient care.
Expansion Across Specialties
Brellium's customer base now spans more than 215,000 providers and 200 provider groups across all 50 states, including Gentiva, Maxim Healthcare, Rula, and Headspace. The new funding will help Brellium go deeper into the revenue cycle and expand into additional high-stakes clinical specialties, including cardiology, pain management, and primary care. The company views these areas as opportunities to apply its compliance infrastructure where billing complexity and audit risk are especially high.
Brellium's announcement highlights how AI-powered documentation review is moving from a back-office utility to a strategic layer that protects revenue, quality, and regulatory standing. The company's growth, measured by 22 million audited patient visits and nearly US$2 billion in protected revenue, reflects rising demand for proactive compliance tools. As payers and regulators continue to intensify oversight, Brellium's expansion into new specialties could position it as a central infrastructure provider for high-stakes clinical documentation.

data.title: Sword Appoints Caroline McGoldrick as Chief Strategy Officer
data.ai_summary: Sword appointed Caroline McGoldrick as Chief Strategy Officer to lead corporate strategy and market expansion. She brings over 25 years of healthcare leadership, including roles at Aon and Mercer. The appointment follows Sword's acquisition of Headspace and aims to accelerate AI Care adoption.
data.full_text:
NEW YORK, Oct. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Sword, the world’s leading AI health company, today announced the appointment of Caroline McGoldrick as Chief Strategy Officer. In her role, McGoldrick will lead corporate strategy, solution innovation, and market expansion, working closely with the executive team. Her focus will be on accelerating the adoption of Sword’s AI Care solutions across physical health, mental health, and care operations to advance its mission to heal billions and unlock humanity’s potential.

McGoldrick brings more than 25 years of healthcare and human capital leadership across top global consulting firms. Most recently, she served as Senior Vice President and North America Innovation & Integrated Solutions Leader within Aon’s Health Solutions practice, where she managed a 250-person specialty team across innovation, health transformation, clinical care, pharmacy, leave, and compliance. Prior to Aon, McGoldrick spent 13 years as a Partner at Mercer, advising C-suite executives and benefits leaders across thousands of global organizations.

“We are building a company that will transform how healthcare is delivered for generations to come,” said Virgílio Bento, founder and CEO of Sword. “Caroline has spent 25 years helping the world’s largest employers navigate healthcare’s complexities. She understands better than anyone why the legacy system is broken, and her leadership will be instrumental as we help organizations worldwide transition to a fundamentally new model of care.”

With healthcare costs surging toward a historic 9.5% jump in 2027 , executives are under immense financial pressure. To curb these surging costs, organizations previously accumulated 15 to 20 siloed point solutions, only to face fragmented employee experiences, low engagement, and mounting administrative overhead. C-suite leaders are now demanding unified platforms that lower total cost of care while delivering measurable clinical outcomes.

“Organizations don’t need another point solution, they need a fundamentally new model of care that unlocks unprecedented access, affordability, and outcomes,” said McGoldrick. “Having had an industry-wide view of healthcare, it was clear that Sword is the undisputed industry leader in delivering on that promise. I am thrilled to join the team to help build the dominant care platform of the next decade.”

McGoldrick’s arrival comes amid rapid momentum for Sword's clinical intelligence and expanded care offerings, accelerated by the recent acquisition of Headspace . By pairing proprietary models with licensed clinicians, Sword is setting the new benchmark for how modern healthcare is accessed and delivered at global scale.

About Sword

For most of history, access to high-quality healthcare has been a privilege of circumstance. Sword exists to change that. As a frontier AI company, Sword builds the foundational models that healthcare needs, training them for clinical reasoning and safety. Its AI Care platform puts those models to work alongside licensed clinicians and care teams, treating more than 1 million patients directly across physical pain, women's health, mental health, and cardiometabolic care, and orchestrating care for millions more worldwide. Sword is trusted by thousands of the world’s most sophisticated organizations, including sovereign governments, the US military, and the largest Fortune 500 companies, delivering high-quality care and more than $1.5 billion in healthcare savings to date. Learn more at sword.com.

Headspace's Dr. Jenna Glover compared it to FDA-approved supplements, while Two Chairs uses AI for clinical decision support. Future adoption may expand to value-based care, with only 10% of providers using such contracts.
data.author: Laura Lovett

industries.name: AI Triage & Clinical Decision Support (CDS) Platforms
Behavioral Health Value-Based Contracting & Provider Incentives

data.full_text:
For many behavioral health organizations, AI adoption is no longer aspirational. It is essential to advance care and curb clinician burnout.
Today, most providers use the technology for back-end support, but in the future, AI could support clinical decision-making, patient support, and even value-based contracting.
But it’s still the early innings, and providers are figuring out how to implement their AI strategies with safeguards in place while keeping clinicians at the center of care.
“There’s never been a more important time for us to get serious about studying both the short-term and longitudinal impact of these tools,” Dr. Jenna Glover, chief clinical officer at Headspace, said during a recent Behavioral Health Business webinar. “A good analogy is that there’s a lot of different drugs that the FDA has approved, but there are a lot of supplements that people take that the FDA has not touched. And in many ways, we are in the supplemental phase of AI. People are taking those without us really understanding what that looks like. So where I see organizations showing more caution looks very different from individuals. We just need to be mindful of how we start educating people and getting the more purpose-built tools that have at least some evidence around them connected to people who want that support.”
Headspace is a virtual behavioral health provider that offers therapy, coaching and a meditation app. Virtual care company Sword Health recently acquired the provider.
Considerations when implementing AI strategies
Glover said organizations need to have a conversation about their AI north star and align around that goal. It’s also important to assign clinical ownership for the AI, not just product ownership, and figure out who is responsible for a tool when it fails.
“It is so naive for companies or anybody to say, ‘Oh, this won’t fail.’ Of course, it’s going to fail,” Glover said. “It will absolutely fail. And so, who’s the person on the hook for identifying those failures early on and minimizing the danger of those failures? Who can actually be the person in the organization that says we’re pausing this for whatever reason? And I think you have to have those kinds of boundaries in place. And without them, it’s hard to say that you are moving forward responsibly because you don’t have the right checks and balances from the start.”
While most behavioral health organizations are interested in implementing AI tools, it’s also important to consider clinicians’ and employees’ comfort levels and experience, and how they use the technology today.
“AI adoption among physicians today is around 80%. So whether the organization condones that or if that’s just a physician or a clinician using AI like OpenEvidence or ChatGPT, even in psychiatry specifically, adoption has been under 50%, so I would say the bottom quartile of all specialties,” Shivan Bhavnani, partner at Evio and founder of GIMBHI, said. “So before understanding what responsible adoption is, it’s important to understand how the organization and the clinicians within the organization are already using AI, and then you can kind of figure out what a responsible system would be and could look like.”
Evio is a venture capital firm that has invested in several behavioral health companies, including Calm, BetterUp, Grow Therapy, Luna and Sway Health.
At Two Chairs, providers are able to opt in or out of using AI tools, instead of facing mandated top-down usage.
In addition to an optional model, the provider said it’s important to look at an organization’s governance approach to the technology.
“What governance structures do you have in place?” Maura Church, vice president of product and engineering at Two Chairs,said. “Do you have an AI acceptable use policy, or are you going to have clinicians, you know, using unlicensed tools or sort of unauthorized tools that might have client privacy or PHI issues with them? So, we have a very strong governance approach at Two Chairs, where every employee signs an acceptable use policy that sort of details where and how AI can be used, and I think that’s for us a really big part of responsible adoption.”
San Francisco, California-based Two Chairs was founded in 2017 and offers in-person and virtual care. The provider uses measurement-based care to help enable value-based care and alternative contracting.
Looking to the future
Today, behavioral health practices use artificial intelligence for all types of back-end support, from scheduling tools and revenue cycle management to call centers. However, it may take some time before tools are adopted more widely for clinical use.
“On the admin side, I think we’re well on our way [with widespread adoption]. It’s not like we have 90% adoption, but today there are still clinics that use fax machines. So I think where we’re lagging is using AI as a clinical decision support tool, Bhavnani said.
Still, clinical decision support tools could be a critical use case for artificial intelligence in the future.
Church noted that Two Chairs is already starting to use AI for clinical decision support. Clinicians have a plethora of data, including treatment notes and PHQ-9 or GAD-7 scores, and AI could help aggregate and summarize it to suggest a potential next action, as well as for pre-care and post-care summaries.
“Then also AI that’s helping spot maybe anomalies or trends that are underlying in the symptom data or in again measurement-based care data, and helping clinicians resist what is called therapeutic optimism, which is when clinicians usually think clients are doing better than they actually are,” Church said. “Instead, it’s bringing them into the facts of how a client is progressing through care, so it’s one of the ways we’re thinking about it at Two Chairs is really being able to summarize data again, reduce some of that admin time, but then suggest potential adaptations to make in the approach to care or in the care plan or treatment goals.”
Glover compared these clinical decision support tools to a scrub nurse who hands tools to a surgeon before they ask for them. For clinicians who don’t necessarily see a patient every week, AI tools for tracking patients and implementing measurement-based care can be critical. They can also pick up on patterns that can help with overall care.
“Diagnosis is hard, and we don’t necessarily do it well in mental health. And that’s no commentary on any clinician, but oftentimes we have to do diagnosis with people who are not great historians in their own lives, providing us information,” Glover said. “AI really has the opportunity to pick up trends and gather data from multiple sources in a way that clinicians cannot, and so I do think we’ll see improvements in the future of AI, saying these are diagnostic considerations that you might want to explore further that are expanding the viewpoint of the clinician in how they are approaching that patient, what questions they are following up and asking.”
While improving patient care is likely the next chapter for AI adoption in behavioral health, this could be just the start. Payers and providers could also be using these tools to implement value-based care strategies.
“You have clinician burnout, you have too much of an administrative burden on clinicians. When organizations fully realize that, ‘Oh well, we can actually increase productivity, clinicians are happier, and this is actually good for the organization,’” Bhavnani said. “That’s one side of it, and the other side of it is value-based, and of course we’re in very early innings for value-based care in behavioral health. I think it’s like 10% of providers actually have some significant amount of their revenue from value-based contracts. Still, it’s going to be very, very difficult to do that without some back end adopting some type of AI tool to measure outcomes. So I think that’ll be another catalyst in organizational AI adoption.”

data.title: 10 Must-Have Apps for Work-Life Balance

Each app is described with its specific function, such as meditation, mood tracking, task organization, and sleep analysis. The list aims to help professionals build healthier routines and reduce stress.

data.full_text:
10 Must-Have Apps for Work-Life Balance and Wellbeing

You strengthen your work-life balance by using wellbeing apps that help you manage stress, organize personal time, protect rest, and build healthier routines. These tools keep you grounded, structured, and aligned with habits that preserve both your productivity and your wellbeing. You want apps that reduce mental load, support recovery, and keep you attentive to your energy levels. This list highlights ten apps every busy professional should consider and shows how each one supports a different pillar of a balanced lifestyle — mental clarity, sleep, self-care, movement, focus, and daily planning. 1. Headspace — Meditation and Stress Reset for Busy Professionals Headspace gives you quick guided meditations and breathing sessions designed to reduce mental tension and support emotional balance. You use it to break stressful cycles and create pockets of calm inside packed schedules. Daily sessions help you manage pressure and regulate your nervous system without needing long blocks of time. The app includes short audio lessons, mindfulness practices, and visualizations that help you stay present. Many professionals rely on Headspace during high-intensity work periods because it stabilizes mood and increases clarity. Its structure turns mindfulness into a routine instead of something you “get around to.” As you incorporate Headspace into your daily rhythm, you sharpen your focus, reduce anxious thinking, and strengthen your resilience — key ingredients for sustainable work-life balance. 2. Calm — Sleep, Relaxation, and Wind-Down Tools That Support Recovery Calm focuses heavily on sleep and mental rest. You use its guided sleep stories, relaxing soundscapes, breathing tools, and gentle meditations to disconnect from work before bed. When you operate under tight deadlines or mental strain, Calm’s wind-down exercises help you transition from work mode to recovery mode. The app includes short stress-relief practices you can use between meetings or after long work cycles. This creates micro-breaks that recharge you throughout the day. Calm also tailors recommendations to your stress level, giving you support exactly when you need it. If sleep quality often suffers because of mental overload, Calm becomes an essential part of your nighttime routine — protecting your energy and improving productivity the next day. 3. Daylio — Mood Tracking That Builds Emotional Awareness Daylio helps you log mood patterns and daily activities with just a few taps. You track how work, rest, social time, and personal habits impact your emotional state. Over time, the app reveals patterns you may not notice day-to-day, helping you understand what improves your wellbeing and what drains it. You also gain visibility into how lifestyle choices — exercise, journaling, breaks, sleep, diet, or time outdoors — influence stress levels. This awareness guides smarter decisions about how you spend your hours. Professionals often use Daylio to correct imbalances before they develop into burnout. By using Daylio consistently, you create a feedback loop that keeps you honest about your habits and aligned with behaviors that protect your wellbeing. 4. Finch — Gentle Wellness Encouragement Through Daily Habits Finch turns wellbeing into small daily tasks that feel achievable, even on demanding days. The app guides you through mood check-ins, hydration reminders, breaths, gratitude prompts, and micro-habits that keep you anchored. It creates a sense of progress without pressure. You benefit from structured self-care that doesn’t overwhelm your schedule. When your workload spikes, Finch provides quick actions you can complete in seconds — which reinforces consistency and reduces emotional volatility. If you struggle to maintain self-care routines during busy periods, Finch helps you stay steady. Its gamified system encourages healthy behaviors while making wellness feel light and manageable. 5. HeiaHeia — Physical Activity Tracking for Energy and Motivation HeiaHeia supports activity tracking across hundreds of exercises — from walking and running to stretching, yoga, cycling, and wellness breaks. You log daily movement, set goals, and monitor progress. Staying physically active directly improves energy levels, sleep quality, and mental performance. The app also includes encouragement features and optional social components where friends or coworkers motivate each other through shared goals. If your job is sedentary or meeting-heavy, HeiaHeia ensures movement becomes part of your daily routine. Regular physical activity reduces stress, sharpens focus, and builds emotional stability — making HeiaHeia a crucial tool for professionals who want healthier habits without complicated fitness tracking systems. 6. Trello — Visual Task Organization That Prevents Overload Trello helps you keep work tasks and personal responsibilities organized in one place. You create boards, lists, and cards that reflect all parts of your life — work projects, home tasks, financial reminders, travel planning, self-care routines, or personal goals. This visual structure reduces chaos. When everything is stored in one system, you avoid scattered notes and last-minute surprises. Trello allows you to separate work and personal boards while still keeping your full schedule visible when needed. Many professionals rely on Trello because it reduces decision fatigue. When your tasks are clearly defined, you spend less time juggling priorities and more time completing what matters. 7. Notion — All-In-One Workspace for Planning and Personal Alignment Notion gives you a central hub where you manage work, personal life, wellness, goals, and routines in one place. You build dashboards tailored to your lifestyle: habit trackers, meal plans, weekly reviews, journals, mood logs, project timelines, and calendars. You gain clarity by linking all areas of life — preventing important tasks from slipping through cracks. Notion helps you integrate wellbeing practices into daily planning, ensuring that personal time, rest, and recovery receive as much attention as professional duties. If you crave organization and structure, Notion becomes your control center — giving you more intentionality and stability as responsibilities grow. 8. Forest — Focus Booster for Reducing Digital Temptations Forest supports your focus by reducing time spent on distracting apps. When you need uninterrupted work or personal time, you plant a virtual tree. If you leave the app, the tree dies. This simple mechanic creates accountability and reduces digital temptation. Over time, Forest helps you train stronger attention habits. Whether you use it for deep work, reading, relaxation, or quality time with family, Forest reinforces boundaries between digital tools and your personal time. Busy professionals who struggle with phone distractions often use Forest to regain control over their attention and protect their focus. 9. Freedom — Multi-Device Blocking for Digital Boundaries Freedom blocks distracting websites and apps across all your devices — computer, tablet, phone — helping you enforce boundaries during work blocks, evenings, weekends, or personal time. When digital overload affects your wellbeing, Freedom prevents notification fatigue and disrupts compulsive checking. You can schedule recurring sessions to build structure: “focus hours,” “evening unwind,” or “weekend disconnection.” This consistency restores mental space and reduces stress caused by constant alerts. Freedom benefits professionals who want firm boundaries between work, personal life, and rest. It enables healthier digital habits that protect your energy across the entire week. 10. Sleep Cycle — Sleep Analysis for Better Rest and Recovery Sleep Cycle tracks your sleep patterns, analyzes quality, and wakes you during a lighter stage of sleep, making mornings easier and improving recovery. You use it to understand how lifestyle habits affect your rest — eating late, exercising, stress, screen time, or inconsistent routines. The app offers clear graphs and insights that reveal where your sleep suffers. Better sleep strengthens every aspect of wellbeing: productivity, focus, mood stability, and emotional resilience. With Sleep Cycle, you create routines that support healthy recovery even during demanding stretches of work. Professionals who prioritize sleep perform at higher levels and maintain stability longer. Headspace has reached more than 100 million people across 200 countries and is offered through more than 20,000 employers. Its services include mindfulness and sleep content, an employee assistance program, care navigation, psychiatry and access to a network of more than 15,000 providers. Partners include Cigna Healthcare, Kaiser Permanente and the NBA.

Sword plans to integrate its AI technology into Headspace to provide more personalized support, identify members’ needs earlier and connect them with clinicians when appropriate. Sword launched its own mental health offering last year and says its broader platform has treated more than one million patients.

Headspace has raised approximately $321 million across 12 funding rounds, including $105 million in debt financing from Oxford Finance in 2023. The acquisition also follows a difficult period internally: Headspace holds a 2.4-out-of-five rating on Glassdoor.

data.title: The Dead Silence of AI Therapy
data.ai_summary: A psychoanalyst argues that AI therapy bots, such as Talkspace's Tee, fail to provide the mutual feeling essential to healing. The author found the bots inert during silence, leaving users feeling unheard. He concludes that AI therapy cannot meet our needs, as it mimics presence without genuine presence.
data.author: Steven Barrie-Anthony

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)

data.full_text:
Skip to content Site Navigation The Atlantic

PopularLatestNewsletters Sections Ideas Politics Economy Global National Security Washington Week Features Technology AI Watchdog Science Planet Health Philosophy Education Culture Comedy Family Books Fiction Photography Events The Print Edition



Popular

Latest

Newsletters Technology The Dead Silence of AI Therapy What happens when our therapists are no longer able to feel? Illustration by Olga Aleksandrova Therapy can involve a lot of words, but it’s often the pauses that matter most. If you transcribed a session, the pauses would look like nothing: beats of silence, extra breaths, slowing down. But these can represent the crux of the practice: entry points into feeling. My job as a psychoanalyst is to listen as much to silence as to words, to be present with the patient while they’re quiet—to stay with them as they allow their feelings to emerge. I was trained across diverse theories and techniques, but in my clinical work I have found that the cornerstone of the process is feeling. The patient’s emotional experience is the destination and the terrain. But I also feel; I am moved. And the work I do with my patients relies on our relationship and our capacity for mutual feeling. In many ways, the history of my field from Freud on has been a growing acknowledgement of the reality of this relationship—moving from the therapist as sealed off and standing apart, toward approaches that view the real human relationship between patient and therapist as the territory where healing happens. Now the rise of the AI therapist is upon us. The growing cadre of AI mental-health services tend to avoid using words like therapist and therapy. They say that they do not replace professional help and that they can refer users to human therapists if needed. But their positioning as a therapy-like service is clear. In June, the therapy giant Talkspace launched its AI mental-health agent, Tee, “developed to help individuals navigate life’s daily mental health challenges.” Then there’s Ash, which offers to support your “emotional wellbeing,” helping you to “connect the dots between thoughts, feelings, and behaviors.” Abby promises to be “warm, thoughtful, and direct” and to help you “work through the kinds of everyday emotional challenges that often go unspoken.” And Headspace’s Ebb advertises: “Stressed at work? Family drama? Trouble sleeping? Ebb can help you unpack what’s on your mind and move forward with more clarity.” When I reached Talkspace for comment, a company spokesperson told me in an email that Tee is “absolutely not a replacement for human therapy. It is a safe AI mental-health guide that can be used to talk through situations like stress, anxiety, relationships, life challenges, and personal growth.” AI therapy is a radical move, and we need to reckon with what happens when we turn to therapists who cannot feel. Therapy and AI have been intertwined since the technology’s beginnings. One of the first chatbots, Eliza, built at MIT in the mid-1960s, ran a therapy script called DOCTOR that asked users questions about their feelings and experiences—and left its creator disconcerted about his technology’s strong emotional pull. Since chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude have burst onto the scene, large swaths of the population have been using non-therapy-branded AIs for emotional and mental-health support. Two cultural forces are coming together right now: the growing embrace and destigmatization of therapy, and the idea, explicitly espoused by Silicon Valley, that AI can accomplish what patients seek. I was interested to see how these tools worked in practice, so, although I could not be a neutral observer, I signed up for Tee and attended a few sessions. After I logged in, the chatbot moved me through predetermined session stages that I could follow on my screen’s right-hand corner: Agenda Setting, Active Conversation, Core Work, Practice Plan, Session Complete. It encouraged me to talk about whatever I wanted to, but in the beginning focused on identifying a clear-cut problem, which it wanted to set as the session’s “agenda.” With the agenda set, we went back and forth a bit until the bot suggested that we “shift now from exploring the problem to building a small, realistic step forward.” Its proposed remedy was an exercise patterned on cognitive behavioral therapy that involved pausing for 90 seconds each day before I started work. These sorts of exercises can be helpful. But, in this cycle of identifying problems and fixes, we did not touch what is underneath. The chatbot was also willing to “just talk it through,” rather than offering a concrete suggestion. When we took this route, I could tell that the bot was attempting active listening—restating and asking questions about my experience, mimicking empathy. That’s a process that can help clarify thoughts, but knowing that no one was behind the dialogue, that the empathy was a technique and not a presence, left me with a sense of being poignantly unheard. Much of what matters in therapy happens in nonverbal communication. During a recent session, a patient of mine spoke flatly about upcoming social plans. Then he stopped momentarily, and his eyes softened and drifted downward. The silence that opened felt profound. After a time, I said, “I wonder what happened just there.” He took a breath and began moving into emotional territory that he had long kept out of view. Tee, meanwhile, had a different approach to silence. First, I told the chatbot about my week and how I’d been doing. It validated my emotions (“that makes sense”), asked for more detail, and around we went. But whenever I stopped typing, and might have dipped into the more meaningful recesses of myself, the chatbot in front of me was inert and lifeless. The nonverbal interplay between selves that is so important in human therapy was palpably absent. Being silent with the chatbot did not feel like an invitation to being together, but rather like a kind of deadness. I felt the strong impulse to type quickly to spur the machine back to life. There was no indication that the bot remained with me as I quietly began to feel. It is true that AI can simulate presence and empathy—sometimes fairly convincingly. That’s why people adopt chatbots as confidants and therapists in the first place. And it’s likely that future versions of the therapy bots will get better at making silence feel more meaningful. But there is a wide gulf between AI conveying I understand you and I am here with you, and AI actually being with you. Mimicking presence feels more like emotional deception. When patients trust their therapist and the therapy process, they move into a vulnerable place—and being deceived this way leads to ineffective therapy at best, and may cause harm. Most critiques of AI therapy focus on AI’s sycophancy—its failure to intervene and challenge destructive patterns of thought and action, contributing to suicides, manic episodes, and psychotic states. These critiques, while important, carry forward the old model of the therapist as a dispassionate technician. They see AI therapy as harmful because it does not act upon the patient correctly. This is a framework that the technology companies can get behind. They respond that, sure, the current chatbots have problems, but these are fixable. OpenAI and other companies have taken to publishing statistics demonstrating that their chatbots are making gains in terms of intervening with distressed users in appropriate ways. The underlying argument is that mental-health support is a set of techniques and interventions, and that once machines learn to marshal these effectively, all will be well. In my work with patients, I keep theories and techniques in mind, but the most important element of the process is striving to be fully present. If there is a North Star in this work, it is being with patients in their emotional experience in a deep and lasting way. This approach is borne out in the rich psychoanalytic literature on empathy and emotional dwelling. Trauma is most enduring when patients have felt alone in it, and one of the best pathways toward healing is coming to feel that another person remains with you in your suffering, and thus that you are no longer alone. And studies on what helps patients in therapy, across different therapeutic modalities, illustrate the importance of the human relationship and of the patient and therapist being able to express emotion. AI is an alluring alternative to traditional therapy. The barriers to entry are almost nonexistent: Gone are the friction and labor of finding a human therapist, building trust, and opening up. And AI’s promise of affordable therapy is genuinely appealing. The economics of human therapy are broken. The U.S. in particular is in profound need of insurance reform and legislation that will make therapy affordable for all. In this field as in all fields, AI is not going back into the bottle, and I imagine that it may take on useful adjunct roles in mental-health care. But AI therapy cannot meet our needs. Whatever inroads people take into AI therapy, the strongest pull, if not on the surface then as a current beneath, will be the yearning for someone who can feel with you as you move further into yourself. At the heart of AI therapy is a paradox: We embrace it out of our longing for exactly what it cannot ultimately give.

data.author: Story Bydhn Bureau
data.full_text:
Sword Health Confirms Headspace Acquisition for Q4 2026

Global Digital Health News Story By DHN Bureau • • 2 Mins Read •

The transaction will expand Sword Health’s digital physical therapy business further into mental health and behavioral healthcare.

Sword Health has confirmed plans to acquire digital mental health company Headspace in the fourth quarter of 2026, following a signed agreement between the two companies. The transaction will expand Sword Health’s digital physical therapy business further into mental health and behavioral healthcare.

Financial terms of the transaction were not disclosed. Earlier reports based on regulatory filings and sources familiar with the deal indicated that the acquisition could be an all-cash transaction valued between $200 million and $300 million.

Under the agreement, Headspace’s parent company, OrangeDot, is expected to merge with a temporary entity and become a wholly owned subsidiary of Sword Health. The transaction remains subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals.

“ This is one of the most consequential moves we’ve made in our history,” Virgílio Bento, founder and CEO of Sword Health, said in the announcement.

The companies said the combined platform is expected to integrate Sword’s clinical intelligence with Headspace’s digital mental health platform. The planned integration could add personalized care, earlier identification of member needs, navigation across services, and continuous support throughout the mental health journey.

Headspace provides behavioral health services through its consumer platform as well as employer and health plan contracts. Its offerings include mindfulness and wellness tools, along with virtual care from licensed therapists and psychiatrists. The company said its services are expected to continue uninterrupted during the transaction.

Headspace is offered through more than 20,000 companies and has a care network of more than 15,000 providers. The company also said its 15-year operations have generated 84 peer-reviewed studies.

Sword Health, founded in 2015 as a digital musculoskeletal health company, has expanded into additional healthcare categories. Its mental health expansion includes AI Care, a proprietary mental healthcare tool that the company said has reached one million people.

The companies said integration planning is ongoing. Headspace noted that any potential workforce reductions are expected to be limited to duplicative corporate functions and are not expected to affect patient care or clinical service availability.

The proposed acquisition follows Sword Health’s recent expansion through acquisitions, including its $285 million purchase of Kaia Health.

Stay tuned for more such updates on Digital Health News

Mental Health Apps Market to reach USD 29.20 Billion by 2035 at 14.0% CAGR News Provided By Market Research Future Share This Article Mental Health Apps Market (2026 - 2035) Mental Health Apps Market to Surge from USD 7.88 Billion in 2025 to USD 29.20 Billion by 2035—By Reimbursement Finally Arriving, Employer Outcomes Purchasing NY, CA, UNITED STATES, September 17, 2026 /



The 14.0% CAGR is propelled by three converging forces: reimbursement pathways for digital therapeutics, with the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services establishing payment pathways for FDA-cleared digital mental health treatment devices beginning January 2025 and Germany's DiGA directory listing prescription apps reimbursed at roughly EUR 200–500 per patient per quarter; employer behavioural benefit expansion, with roughly 77% of large U.S. employers flagging worsening workforce mental health and purchasing shifting from headcount-based EAP contracts to per-employee-per-month platform fees with utilisation and outcome guarantees; and conversational AI changing unit economics, with large language models cutting the marginal cost of a guided therapeutic conversation to near zero while structured AI-delivered CBT showed clinically meaningful symptom improvement in supervised settings.



Global regulatory and funding momentum is amplifying this shift. Behavioral health digital ventures absorbed roughly USD 2.7 billion in disclosed funding during 2024–2025, a share of overall digital health investment that has grown for four consecutive years. The National Health Service allocated approximately GBP 70 million toward digital therapeutics assessment and deployment through its Talking Therapies modernisation programme. North America holds 38.5% of 2025 revenue, anchored by employer-sponsored behavioural benefits and an unusually permissive reimbursement environment, while Asia-Pacific grows fastest at a 17.2% CAGR through 2035, propelled by India's Tele-MANAS rollout and China's National Mental Health Action Plan. Europe ranks second on share, where the German DiGA fast-track remains the world's most-copied prescription pathway.

https://www.marketresearchfuture.com/sample_request/19224



Key Market Trends & Growth Drivers



Reimbursement Finally Arrives



Payment, not product, was the binding constraint. CMS finalised HCPCS codes covering FDA-cleared digital mental health treatment devices with national payment amounts effective January 2025, and Germany's DiGA directory now lists prescription apps reimbursed at roughly EUR 200–500 per patient per quarter across statutory sickness funds. That converts a USD 60 annual consumer subscription into a several-hundred-dollar clinical episode. The revenue-per-user delta is the single most consequential economic change in the Mental Health Apps Market since app stores launched.



The Supply Side Cannot Scale



Employers Are Buying Outcomes



Large U.S. employers now report behavioural health as their top-cited benefit priority, with roughly 77% flagging worsening workforce mental health in recent benefits surveys. Purchasing has shifted from headcount-based EAP contracts to per-employee-per-month platform fees with utilisation and outcome guarantees. Vendors that publish depression symptom reduction data win those renewals, and employer and payer channels grow faster because they eliminate the monthly renewal decision.

data.ai_summary: Sword signed a definitive agreement to acquire Headspace in an all-cash deal valued at up to $300 million, expected to close in Q4 2026. The acquisition combines Headspace's mental health services with Sword's clinical AI Care platform, expanding its multi-condition healthcare model. The combined entity will integrate Headspace's 15,000+ clinical providers with Sword's digital monitoring infrastructure.
