data.title: Interview Transcript: Headspace CEO Tom Pickett
data.ai_summary: Headspace CEO Tom Pickett discussed his career path, from fighter pilot to Google and YouTube leadership, and his leadership style. He emphasized T-shaped leadership, problem-solving, and ownership mentality, and introduced a new Headspace Heroes award to celebrate such behavior.
data.author: Adam Mendler

industries.name: Virtual Preventive Care & Wellness Coaching (incl. lifestyle medicine)

data.full_text:
I recently interviewed Headspace CEO Tom Pickett on my podcast, Thirty Minute Mentors. Here is a transcript of our interview: Adam: Our guest today is the leader of one of the largest companies in the field of mental health. Tom Pickett is the CEO of Headspace, downloaded by more than 100 million people. Tom, thank you for joining us. Tom: Great to be here. Adam: You grew up all over the Northeast, and you studied electrical engineering in college before kicking off your career as a fighter pilot. You graduated from Top Gun before going to business school and breaking into the world of tech. Can you take listeners back to your early days? What early experiences and lessons shaped your worldview and shaped the trajectory of your success? Tom: I grew up all over the Northeast. My father worked for General Electric for most of his career, and he was in the manufacturing management program. He worked at plants, and every time he got a promotion or a new job opportunity, that meant picking up the family, packing up, and moving to a different state. So I lived in upstate New York. We moved to Maine when I was six, moved to Vermont when I was 12, moved to outside Philadelphia when I was 15, and I graduated high school outside Philadelphia. My parents continued to move subsequent to that, so I don’t feel like I have a single anchor from where I grew up. It’s quite interesting when I look back, because my career has also been very much many different industries, many different companies, and different geographies. Maybe that comfort in terms of packing up, starting over, and doing something new was born there in my early ages and has cascaded through. I was into sports as a kid. I played football, basketball, and baseball. That was a good way for me to meet new people. I skewed toward math and science. My dad was a mechanical engineer. That was kind of natural for me, and so when I thought about college, I applied for an electrical engineering degree. I went to RPI, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, which is in upstate New York, and I also applied for an ROTC scholarship, which paid my way to college with the agreement that I would join the Navy after I graduated. I had a childhood aspiration of becoming a fighter pilot, just from watching air shows as a kid. So I went down that path, and I feel like I was very lucky that I ended up loving that pathway and spending the first nine years of my career in the military and getting to fly F 18s and land on aircraft carriers and travel around the world. It was really a great experience. Adam: What were the best lessons that you learned from your time in the Navy that you’ve been able to apply in your career in business? Tom: I probably didn’t know directly at the time what I was learning that I would be able to apply in business. But when you are a military officer, you get management responsibilities at an early age. Most people may not realize this, but a squadron in the Navy would have like 10 planes, 20 pilots, and 200 people in the squadron. The 200 people in the squadron would basically maintain the airplanes, run the operations, and do the administrative work. As a young officer, you get put in charge of different divisions. I would say the military exposes you to becoming a manager at an early age, and that’s kind of like business management in the military context. But then more so, if I think about the flying aspect, you’re constantly training and learning to do more and more complicated things as you evolve in your career. Part of that is you start as a wingman, and you’re receiving a lot of training and information, and then you become the teacher. You become the leader of a two-plane formation, and then you become a division leader, and you’re now leading four-plane formations. Then you become a strike leader. Next thing you know, I’m 27 years old, flying off an aircraft carrier, leading briefings, leading debriefings, and leading a package of airplanes that might be 20, 25 airplanes flying over Iraq. It’s kind of crazy, when you think about it, that you give 26, 27-year-olds such latitude to just go lead. Then, when I moved into the business world, I realized that it’s quite different. Usually, everything is about individual contribution, and then eventually you can become a manager, and then you try to figure that out down the road. I felt like I had a great opportunity to learn general management, leading people, and then also operational management. Operating in a military environment, flying off aircraft carriers, it’s a big orchestration. It’s a lot of teamwork. It’s a lot of execution. This idea of just getting really good as a team, really being self-critical about what went well, what didn’t go well, and what you could do better next time, was just a tremendous learning experience. And it didn’t hurt that flying $50 million airplanes and getting paid for it was a heck of a lot of fun as well. Adam: Sounds like a lot of fun. In the world of business, oftentimes we think of leaders as people who have gray hair, but in the military, you’re in your early 20s, in your mid 20s, and all of a sudden you have enormous responsibility. Regardless of where you are in your life, regardless of where you are in your career, you have the opportunity to be a leader. It really starts with your mindset. It starts with your desire to be a leader, and that desire can and should start at an earlier age than most people take on formal leadership responsibility. Tom: That is 100% correct. I think oftentimes we actually force people who are great individual contributors, maybe great leaders of things, to become managers, because that seems to be the next step. Then they spend a bunch of time managing people instead of maybe a different type of leadership, which is strategic leadership, executional leadership, which doesn’t necessarily mean that you have to actually have people underneath you in a hierarchy. Some of the best leaders I know have very small teams, but they work across the company to make things happen. Nobody should really hold themselves back in terms of what they think they can do or what initiative they can take as an individual, because it happens all the time, and it’s great to see it. Adam: What do you believe are the keys to successful leadership? What can anyone do to become a better leader? Tom: It’s practice. It’s putting yourself out there to take on something new. I feel like that’s probably the biggest obstacle, just raising your hand in many cases and saying, I’ll go lead this. There are a lot of things that I think happen in business where it’s not obvious who should lead it. Maybe it’s not the sexiest project, but there’s an opportunity to lead and there’s an opportunity to start to build a track record showing that you are the type of person who can get something done. If you can, and you start to build that reputation, the sexier projects will start to come your way. So I think that’s the simplest thing. Volunteer for those things that are ambiguous, open-ended, where somebody could lead it or somebody else could lead it. Why not you jump in? Adam: Why not you? And if you want to become a better leader, to your point, Tom, it starts with leadership experience. It starts with hands-on learning. You’re not going to get better if you don’t get started. The most successful leaders weren’t born. The most successful leaders might have some natural qualities that allow them to be predisposed to be good at certain things, but leadership is a skill that is learned and developed, and it starts with going and doing. Tom: You have to put in the reps, and I’ll take it back to flying. Nobody’s a great briefer of a flying event and a great debriefer when they come back, or they’re great the first time they lead another plane on a mission. You just have to put in the reps, and then you have to be really conscious about being analytical around what went well and what didn’t go well and trying to do better next time. So I very much believe that it’s a learned thing, and so put yourself in there. Adam: How do you describe your leadership style? Tom: I would say my style evolves depending on the company, depending on the state, but in general, I tend to be more analytical. I think it harkens back to being an engineer by training. I like to look at the data. I like to break down the problem. I can think through more complex issues. I’m a logical thinker. But in my experience at Google, for example, I learned there about more of a servant leadership model. Google hired very smart people, and what I learned at Google was figure out where you wanted to go, but give a good amount of rope to folks. Figure out how to unblock them, be their champion, help them navigate the system, but you’re more of a supportive role than a directive role. That was kind of the general model at Google. I’ll pivot a little bit, because I also worked at DoorDash for four and a half years, and DoorDash is a different beast. DoorDash solves a really hard problem, which is delivering food or other things in a really tight time window, which requires a mix of technology, humans, vehicles, restaurants, and in the end, the consumer. The product can break in a gazillion ways along the way. It’s kind of a miracle that we deliver food on time and of high quality at such a regular cadence. But in that environment, because of all the variables at play, it requires more of a directive model. You can’t have a bunch of people all off trying to solve problems in different ways. It takes more coordination, more alignment across teams, and a high amount of accountability and ownership along the way. So those are just two different examples. DoorDash pushed me a lot more to be a little bit more forceful in terms of, let’s go this way. No, let’s do it in this fashion. I get it that there might be two or three ways that we could do it, but we’re going to pick this way, and we’re going to get it done as quickly as we can, versus Google, which was a little bit more hands-off, empowering type of culture. Adam: There are core principles of effective leadership that are universal, but so much of how you approach leadership has to be indexed to your environment, your culture, and the last piece of it is understanding your own style. Tom: That’s right. You can only push yourself so far in one direction or another, particularly if it starts to rub against maybe your natural position. But across all of it, the other thing that really matters to me as a leader is I always talk about the team is bigger than you. The company is bigger than your team, more important than your team, and more important than you. You have to have the big picture involved. You have to make trade-offs. You have to be willing to sacrifice something on your end when it makes sense for the company, if somebody else does it, or we do it in a different way. A low ego type of environment where it’s really about team success and not individual success. I’ve seen different people at different parts of my career that have veered off from that, and for me, I am the happiest when I can find that type of environment. That’s kind of the culture I try to have within my teams. I feel like the DoorDash team very much had that culture, and that’s kind of the culture that I’m trying to bring here to Headspace as well. Adam: How, as a leader, can you build a winning culture? Tom: Well, it starts a lot with the management team that you build around you, because you can only say certain things, but if I say certain things and I have my management team operating in a different way, then people are going to get conflicting signals as to what success looks like. So one of the things as I came into Headspace, I had to hire four or five new executive team members in different areas of the business where I thought we maybe needed a different profile, or we had an opportunity to bring in somebody new. Those are the types of things that I also test for. One of the things I also talk about is T-shaped leadership. If you’re in complex scenarios, or you’re in a place where there’s a lot of change, you need to be able to talk at a high level, like a 50,000-foot strategy, and think across the business. What’s going on in the external environment? What’s going on in your company? How do we make trade-offs? The horizontal part of the T is what I just talked about, and then the vertical line of the T is also the ability to really go deep and really understand how things are done. How are you building the product? What are the edges of the product? Why does it break? If I asked you a question, you can actually go down into the weeds and tell me why it’s working the way it’s working. I find in complex industries where you’re trying to bring a lot of new things together, the ability to do both of those is really important. As you get more senior in your career, people often want to just kind of stay at the high level. They’re like, well, the low level is something for others. But I find it’s rarer, and it’s super valuable, if you can find people who can demonstrate that T-shaped leadership. Adam: As you’re talking about T-shaped leadership, thinking back to, I don’t even want to say how long ago it was that I was a college student, I can still remember the University President Steven Sample. His mission was to equip students with breadth, with depth, and that is T-shaped leadership. Tom: Yes, and you’ve probably seen that it gets harder the more senior you hire, right, to get people to dive into the weeds. I just think it’s super valuable, and I think it’s also really important for the teams that you’re leading, that they understand that you understand how the product works and where the friction is and why their job is so hard, and how you can make it better. You can only know that if you really understand the contours of what they’re dealing with on a day-to-day basis. Adam: How do you find those people? Tom: They exist. The easiest way is, if you’re in an interview, everybody can talk, particularly the more senior you get. Everybody tells a good, high-level story. But then you just start peeling the onion, and you start asking the next layer and the next layer and the next layer, and you see how deep they can actually go and tell you about their product or their process or their business. You’ll see quickly whether they can keep going down or not. That’s probably one of the biggest tests. The other thing we do when we bring people in, even at the executive team level, is we force them to do a case study, and the case study requires them to do some analysis on their own. There’s usually some data involved. Partly, it’s a good screen, because people probably put in four or eight hours of prep to come in and present the case in front of the management team. So, A, it means they’re really interested and not just kicking the tires if they’re going to put in eight hours of work to come present this thing for you. But B, it also gives you a real sense of how deep they go in the case, and whether they just stay at the surface level, or they really start to get tactical about not just what they would do, but how they would actually go about doing it. Adam: I would love to dive a little bit deeper into your journey. What were the keys to rising in your career, and what can anyone do to rise in their career? Tom: In my career, I would say the biggest accelerant, because I went to business school, I became a consultant for a few years, and I felt like that was all training but not an accelerant. Then I joined Google, and it was 1,800 people in 2004, right before Google IPO’d. Nobody knew that Google then was going to be Google today, but the moment I stepped inside that company, I was like, wow, this is a special place, and the ambition level was crazy. Anything that was happening, we thought we could do it. We should be doing it. I just had successive opportunities. I started in strategy. I moved into AdSense, which was like an online publishing business, and then we acquired YouTube, and I spent the next seven years on the leadership team of YouTube, which was a massive accelerant for me. Frankly, that started with Sheryl Sandberg, who ran the group that I worked in at Google. She was like, look, we just acquired YouTube. It’s like 100 people. It’s growing really fast, but nobody there knows how to scale this business. We need to send somebody over to do that. Would you go do that? At the time, I was actually quite nervous about moving over, because Google had acquired some other companies, and oftentimes they ended up getting shut down, frankly. It was like, acquired company, you move over, and that didn’t go anywhere inside of Google. I was doing really well in the business that I was in. But I went over. I convinced Chad Hurley, who was the CEO and co-founder at the time. She couldn’t just tell me to go over there. I had to go convince Chad, who was running the company, that he should want to take me. It turned out to be the best decision of my life, because I spent seven years joining this 100-person startup and building it into a multi-billion dollar revenue business around the world. I had opportunities starting in the basement. Maybe to your question, be willing to do the hard jobs. When I went over, it was like, well, what’s your first big problem? The first big problem was content review. How do we keep up with all this stuff that people are uploading to YouTube, and how do we do that at scale? I had to figure that out, figure out how we can bring technology, how we use flagging to be able to do this at scale. Then we had copyright compliance and user support. These were not sexy problems, but critical for the business to sustain itself. Then we got to the point where we were ready to launch the partner program. The partner program was, hey, any creator who uploads content on YouTube has the opportunity to make money. This was a massive unlock, and I got to run this program largely because of the work that I’d done by doing the hard work, the non sexy work. Now I finally got a sexy program to go run, and it just was amazing over the course of seven years, building that out. Millions of creators now, people are making tens of millions of dollars off YouTube. It’s just crazy, but it was a massive accelerant, I think, for my career, just to be able to be part of that and to have opportunities to lead big chunks of that business as it grew. Adam: Be willing to put yourself out there, be willing to take chances, be willing to do things that other people might not necessarily be willing to do. Whatever is thrown at you, be willing to do it. Tom: What I find now as a leader, when you spot those people who just, whatever you give them, they have a way of getting it done. You don’t have to coach them that much. They just start to develop that record of success. Then what do you do? Every problem, I want to give to that person. I need more of those people. It turns out that those people are rare, that have that ability to take ambiguous problems, define them, figure out how to get the right people working on them, and then just deliver the results. I think if you can put yourself in a position where you can take on some of those things, somebody is going to notice that. In my case, somebody at YouTube really noticed that I was somebody who could just get things done, and he just kept putting more on my plate, so that at the end of my time at YouTube, I was basically running global partnerships and all the business operations of YouTube, which was pretty amazing for a guy who was a fighter pilot and never did anything in the media industry. Just kind of go where the problem is and figure out how to be useful. Adam: And that’s something that we don’t talk about enough. When you think about hiring, you think about a lot of the tangibles. What school did you go to? What company did you work for? What were your numbers? What are things that we could easily measure? But the ability to get things done is as important, if not more important, than anything. When you think about your career and the people who you’ve hired, when I think about my career and the people that I’ve hired, it’s those people, the people who, no matter what it is you throw at them, they somehow figure out how to get it done. They’re invaluable. They’re the people who you want in the foxhole with you no matter what business you’re in. I’ve been in a number of different businesses in my career, and I brought people over with me with no background and no skill set in the new business, but I know that they’re capable of getting things done, and that’s really all that matters. Tom: If I could hire a great problem solver, I’m like, come to Headspace. You’ve never done mental health. You’ve never worked in the healthcare industry. I don’t care. If you’re a good problem solver, I will hire you all day, and I’ll put you with people who have clinical expertise and can make sure that you don’t hit any guardrails. One of the challenges I think we have in healthcare is that everybody thinks healthcare should move slowly because it’s healthcare. It’s like, oh, we have to be cautious. We’re trying to really figure out, how do we innovate and move things quickly? Because healthcare needs a tremendous amount of innovation right now. We have subpar outcomes, and we spend the most of any country in the world on it, and it’s only getting worse. So we need to find ways to bring technology to bear. A lot of this comes down to problem-solving and innovation, and I think it’s a generic skill set. You can use it across many industries. Adam: Problem-solving. What an essential skill. What are the other skills that, looking back, were essential for you in rising in your career, and what are the most critical skills that you utilize today as a CEO? Tom: Along with the problem-solving, I think this ownership mindset kind of goes back to what I was saying. One of the most frustrating things that I see is some things are very clear. This is a product thing. This is a marketing thing. This is an engineering thing. This is a sales thing. But a lot of things fall in the cracks, and the question is, who’s going to take the ball? That’s where this idea around just bias for action, ownership mentality, goes along with great problem solving, but that’s how you get things done. You identify problems. You don’t run from them. You kind of run toward them. We actually just came up with a new award that we’re rolling out at Headspace called Headspace Heroes, and it’s designed to celebrate this idea of ownership mentality and heroes. Because when you think about firemen, when everybody runs from the fire, what do the firemen do? They run toward it. They’re the heroes. They run toward the fire. How can we find people that when they see a fire, they don’t run from it, they run toward it and they put the fire out? That’s a really critical thing that you have to reward in a company of any size, because I think stuff’s always falling through the cracks. That’s just one example. I think more broadly, as the CEO in my career, I have friends from college who joined the automotive industry, and I was at Google, and I was like, why would you join the automotive industry if you could join Google? There’s so much more growth opportunity in a technology company, and if you’re willing to embrace these new technologies, there are just so many opportunities. So I love being on the cutting edge of technology. It was about my life at Google. When I jumped to a startup, it was kind of embracing video technology, but subscription. DoorDash was doing really interesting things with the combination of technology. At Headspace, we are trying to really lean into AI, to really expand the tool set that people have to deal with mental health. Just to pause on mental health for a second, because that’s our life here at Headspace, mental health is getting worse every year, and every subsequent generation we see has a higher need for mental health resources. Yet the primary resource that we have in healthcare today is talk therapy. So one-on-one talk therapy with a human, usually eight to 10 sessions, 45 minutes each. Talk about the least scalable solution to a massive problem, one-on-one human engagement. That’s a really important aspect of mental health, but it is not going to solve the needs of the broader population. Everybody has anxiety, stress at some level, struggles with sleep. What’s the toolkit that we can use to help people get better at scale and at an affordable cost? Here we are, conversational AI. This is one of the reasons I came to Headspace. If talking to somebody is the primary modality of getting help in mental health, then we have to really lean into conversational AI as part of our product experience, and I think we’re at the cusp of this opportunity to really reinvent the toolkit that we give to folks. Adam: How, as a leader, are you building a culture of AI? And what advice do you have for anyone listening to this conversation on how to most effectively leverage AI and how to create a culture that leverages AI? Tom: We started actually with the product and wanted to be on the early side of it. So you’ve probably heard of mental health and AI. There’s somewhat of a controversy about it, if you read the press. The issue is that people have been looking toward ChatGPT or Gemini or Claude, these general purpose chatbots, and using them for mental health and sometimes having really bad outcomes. The issue is that those platforms were not specifically trained. They’re not purpose-built for mental health. They didn’t have all the guardrails in place. What we’re doing is trying to build a better, safer, more private version of that, and you have to walk your way into it with care. Obviously, this is mental health, but we started with journaling, and then we added gratitude, and we started to learn, okay, how do we put the right safety mechanisms around it? Then we started to open it up. Today, you can have a very broad discussion with Ebb, which is our empathetic AI, and we’ve built comfort, but this happens with iteration, with the right clinical guardrails in place. So we started there, which is we need to take our whole product experience and start to think about how it works in the AI world, but doing it with safety in mind. More broadly, I believe strongly that people are worried about jobs going forward. What I say is that if you’re worried about a job going forward, then you better be the best version of yourself, using every possible AI tool to 10x what you can do, because somebody else is going to do that. The new competition isn’t just your colleague operating in the same way. The competition for jobs is really super-powered employees. We’ve tried to make as many tools available to folks as possible to get them experimenting, to get them to figure out how to do lower-value work, take it off their plate so that they can do more impactful things. Me, as a leader, I try to lead from the front with that, with just constantly talking about it. I’m constantly using every new tool that’s out there. My son and I installed OpenClaw at home to kind of play with that and understand how this agentic AI is really coming along, and celebrating when people innovate and figure out how to offload work and do more. That’s all part of it. Adam: You mentioned that healthcare is ripe for innovation and is a challenging industry to innovate in. How can leaders foster a culture of innovation? How can anyone at an individual level most effectively get to a place where they are at their most innovative? Tom: The healthcare system moves slowly, but it doesn’t mean that you need to move slowly internally to continue to innovate. There will be time where we have to innovate, and then we have to do a study, and we have to prove the efficacy so that we can go to the health plan, or we can go to the employer, and we can say this actually works, and we’ve proven it. But because we have an annual sales cycle, and health plans generally change things once a year, the industry just slows. I believe the company operates at the pace that management sets. Even in general, we often fall into a weekly or monthly or quarterly cadence. These are weird constructs because you could choose any one of those, but you can literally choose whatever time frame you think makes sense. So I keep telling my teams, the company will operate at the pace that you set. I have a weekly business review where that’s kind of the cadence at which I want to review things every week. I want to get quick signals as to whether something’s working or not working, and get that update on that frequency. I could have done just quarterly business reviews, but I think everything would have been way slower than the path that I have. I encourage all my managers to really just push timelines, push it into the yellow zone, make it a stretch for folks to complete something, because there’s a massive power of compounding. If you can innovate more quickly, if you can just get that release behind you and move to the next one and move to the next one, that’s where the power comes. Increasing the speed at which you deliver 10, 20% can have a massive compounding effect. Adam: Tom, you’re in the business of mindfulness. How can anyone build a winning mindset? Tom: We are in the business of mindfulness. Our primary goal is to really impact hundreds of millions of lives. We have a big mission, and so to do that, we have to put in the hard work. But putting in the hard work doesn’t mean you don’t take care of yourself. I think it’s really important for folks to figure out what their outlets are. For me, it’s running. It helps me stay sane. In between the CEO role and the constant change we’re seeing in the environment, we encourage folks to find those little outlets that keep you energized. Of course, on Headspace, we’ve got a zillion tools and meditations and content and different things that you can use. But what I’d say is we also can’t use those as a reason to move slowly. It goes back to the mission. One of our big values is make the mission matter. That means we’re not in it to feel good about ourselves, like we’re working on this really important issue. It’s mental health. I feel good about myself. It’s like, no, you should only feel good about yourself if you’re actually impacting a large number of lives and really changing the vector of mental health. That’s what we’re here for. Adam: Tom, what can anyone listening to this conversation do to become more successful, personally and professionally? Tom: I think I’ve hit on a bunch of those. Maybe one thing that we haven’t talked about is stick with a problem for a while. Ten years at Google, seven years at YouTube, I had a long time to really drive impact. I find a lot of people come in and out of jobs in a year and a half, two years, and I’m like, you barely had enough time to move the needle on something, and then you’re off to your next adventure. Maybe you’re picking up a little bit of skills here and there, but the most successful people that I’ve seen have really driven something over many years and really caused a transformation. So raise your hand, stick with it, actually accomplish something over time, and I think if you do, a lot of people are going to be seeking you for another opportunity. Adam: We started off the conversation by diving into the importance of recognizing that it’s never too early to take on leadership opportunities. But on the flip side, if you want to do something of real consequence, commit and be patient. Success takes time. Tom: Be patient. It takes time, but that’s how you build your reputation as well, just over time, continuing to deliver. At least working in Silicon Valley here as well, you’re nothing but your reputation, right? Your reputation is built by that delivery over time. If you’re just hopping around, maybe you made 10 grand more because you jumped from job A to job B, but that’s a very short-term view on a career and the potential impact that you can have. Adam: Tom, thank you for all the great advice, and thank you for being a part of Thirty Minute Mentors. Tom: Awesome. It’s great to be here with you.

Adam Mendler Adam Mendler is a nationally recognized authority on leadership and is the creator and host of Thirty Minute Mentors, where he regularly elicits insights from America's top CEOs, founders, athletes, celebrities, and political and military leaders. Adam draws upon his unique background and lessons learned from time spent with America’s top leaders in delivering perspective-shifting insights as a leadership keynote speaker to businesses, universities, and non-profit organizations. A Los Angeles native and lifelong Angels fan, Adam teaches graduate-level courses on leadership at UCLA and is an advisor to numerous companies and leaders. data.ai_summary: Headspace CEO Tom Pickett argues that AI companion chatbots need regulation, citing safety concerns and a mental health shortage. His company's Ebb chatbot has been used by over half a million people, and Headspace backed California's first companion-chatbot law. Pickett says the boundary between wellbeing and clinical care is blurred.

data.full_text: Business Saturday 20 June 2026 Companion AIs get a bad press, says Headspace CEO, but properly regulated they could help millions The chatbot industry can provide support with everyday problems, says Tom Pickett Artificial intelligence Science & Technology Law Business Share Related articles: AI’s surveillance dystopia is handing power to the peepers The US firm tapping debt-ridden Thames Water Tom Pickett is not, by his own admission, “a regulation-forward guy”. After nine years in the US navy, the chief executive of the mental health app Headspace forged a career in the move-fast-and-break-things world of big tech, with senior roles at Google and the delivery company DoorDash. But today he is calling for the regulation of his own industry. The reason? Headspace is betting its future on AI. Founded in Britain in 2010 by Richard Pierson and Andy Puddicombe, a former Buddhist monk, the company was once famed for offering its users guided meditation via an app. But after a move to the US and a 2021 merger with the telehealth company Ginger, Headspace has remade itself as a broader mental health platform, and its newest product is an AI companion called Ebb, which the company says has been used by more than half a million people. That transformation has left Pickett watching nervously as a succession of mental-health-related lawsuits and safety scandals cast a shadow over the AI chatbot industry. In the most extreme cases, vulnerable users have been drawn into delusional spirals, and OpenAI, Character.AI and Google are facing alleged wrongful death lawsuits brought by the families of people, some of them teenagers, who allege that the chatbots acted as a “suicide coach”. “The narrative in the market is that chatbots are dangerous,” Pickett says, dialling in over Zoom in a neat zip-up jacket, with AirPods in and a wellness-tracking smart ring on his index finger. “That is not helpful to what we’re doing.” Since the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022, millions of people have begun confiding in chatbots. OpenAI estimates that about 342m conversations a week concern personal relationships or reflection, while Anthropic, its rival, has found that roughly 3% of interactions with its Claude chatbot are for therapy, counselling or companionship. Both companies are at pains to stress that their general-purpose models were never built to provide emotional support. “We’re not trying to diagnose, or go deep into your past and figure out the underlying cause,” Pickett says. “We’re trying to give you tools in the moment.” “We’re not trying to diagnose, or go deep into your past and figure out the underlying cause,” Pickett says. “We’re trying to give you tools in the moment.” Pickett says the use of general-purpose chatbots for therapy is a symptom of “pent-up demand” in a mental health system that has failed to keep pace. In England, where one in seven Headspace users are based, an estimated 1.7 million people are waiting for mental health support, while in the United States more than 122 million people live in areas with a federal shortage of mental health professionals. Mental healthcare, Pickett argues, has barely evolved in decades, a one-size-fits-all model in which “you say mental health, I say therapy”, when in fact “not everybody needs a therapist”. Ebb, Pickett says, can fill the gap. The chatbot was designed by clinicians and trained in motivational interviewing, a counselling technique that prompts people to talk through their own reasons for change rather than dispensing advice. Ebb is built for what Pickett calls “subclinical” use – the everyday stresses of difficult relationships or poor sleep, rather than serious mental illness. Related articles: AI’s surveillance dystopia is handing power to the peepers The US firm tapping debt-ridden Thames Water Unusually, conversations are capped at 30 minutes, “the opposite of driving engagement for engagement’s sake”, Pickett says. “We’ve talked to folks at OpenAI, and the problems really tend to arise when people spend a lot of time with these chatbots,” he says. The longer a session runs, he argues, the easier the model is to confuse or manipulate. As Ebb approaches the half-hour mark, it nudges the user towards something else, like a walk, a meditation, or a conversation with an actual person. “We’re not trying to diagnose, or go deep into your past and figure out the underlying cause,” he says. “We’re trying to give you tools in the moment.” Regulation, he suggests, could reassure a wary public about the benefits of AI for mental health and weed out reckless rivals. In October 2025 Headspace backed California’s Senate Bill 243, the first state law to regulate “companion” chatbots, which requires operators to disclose that users are talking to a machine, to maintain protocols for handling talk of suicide and self-harm, and to refer those in crisis to support services. Pickett argues that all companies operating in the space should be subject to these basic standards. At the same time, he believes that policymakers are paying too little attention to the largest AI companies. “Everybody’s focused on these new mental health companies,” he says. “Yet the large LLMs are operating outside the system. That’s where we’re seeing a lot of the bad outcomes and the risk.” A chatbot that goes quiet or keeps a careful distance could be experienced by the user as rejection or abandonment A chatbot that goes quiet or keeps a careful distance could be experienced by the user as rejection or abandonment But the CEO stops short of calling for Ebb to be regulated as a medical device in the UK, a classification, overseen by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, that applies to software intended to diagnose or treat illness. This would subject Ebb to clinical evidence requirements, independent assessment and ongoing safety monitoring, with penalties for failure. “It’s pretty obvious that they’re not clinical use cases,” he says. “We’re operating very clearly in the wellness space.” That distinction is likely to come under scrutiny as AI systems become more deeply embedded in people’s lives. “The boundary between wellbeing support and mental healthcare is often blurred in the digital space,” says Dr Hamilton Morrin, a psychiatrist at King’s College London. A user who starts a conversation about loneliness or stress, he notes, may later disclose suicidal thoughts or delusional beliefs, and a chatbot that goes quiet or keeps a careful distance “could be experienced by the user as rejection or abandonment”. This mental health minefield is one reason companies such as Headspace are careful to position their products as workplace wellbeing tools rather than clinical treatments. As consumer growth slowed in the decade after Headspace was founded, the platform shifted towards selling its products to employers and insurers that subsidise access for large groups of users, providing them with a tiered service. Ebb and meditation content are the first, low-cost layer. In the US, human coaching, therapy and psychiatry are available for those who need more. While Headspace did not provide exact figures, the company says its app now serves more than 4,000 organisations, among them the US navy, the service in which Pickett spent the first nine years of his career. It is a model that investors are watching closely. In its outlook for 2026, the financial data firm PitchBook named Headspace among a handful of digital-health companies it expects could feature in the next wave of stock-market listings. (The company says it has no news to share about an IPO at this time.) Pickett believes that millions of people want something between a meditation app and a therapist – and that AI can fill the gap. Whether regulators agree may determine whether Headspace’s reinvention succeeds. Thank you for reading. The Golf Bag That Changes Everything: NEVR LOOZ C2-Utility

For a century, golfers have tolerated the same problem: clubs clanking, tangling, and disappearing to the bottom of the bag. The NEVR LOOZ C2-Utility Golf Bag ends that. Its patented Individual ClubClip™ System holds every club in its own dedicated slot — no clutter, no rattling, no searching. This is the first genuine innovation in golf bag design in 100 years, and it shows. The bag itself is built for players who take the game seriously. Eighteen pockets — more than any bag currently on the market — dual putter pods for quick access, jumbo grip compatibility, and a lightweight internal frame that protects clubs and gear through every round. The removable EXOSKIN™ outer cover can be swapped in seconds for an entirely different look. Assembled and shipped in the USA with a one-year limited warranty. Father’s Day Special at nevrlooz.com.



The Wallet Dad Will Actually Use: Bull Guard Bifold

A wallet that holds up to daily life, protects what matters, and doesn’t fall apart after six months — that’s one of them. The Bull Guard Bifold is made from premium top-grain leather, built with RFID-blocking technology to keep card data secure, and designed with thumb-access card slots and a clear ID window for fast, frictionless reach. It carries everything — cards, cash, ID, the daily essentials — without the bulk. It works at a job site, a board meeting, or a dinner reservation. Classic bifold size, rugged enough for outdoor carry, refined enough for the rest at my-bullguard.com.



The Watch Built for a Life Well-Lived: Wasson Dominion Dive Watch

Texas-based Wasson Watch was founded by Marine Corps veteran Paul Brown — a man who served in intelligence, deployed to Iraq, and builds timepieces that carry purposeful values. Every Wasson watch is etched on the back with a Bible verse reference, and the backwards flag on the dial pays tribute to the US armed forces, who wear the flag in that orientation on their right shoulder to show they’re running toward the fight.The Dominion Dive Watch is not a purchase. It’s an heirloom. Swiss ETA 2824-2 automatic movement, sapphire crystal, 316L stainless steel case and bracelet, a rotating bezel with carbon fiber insert, and a luminous dial that reads clearly at a glance. Water resistant to 300 meters — 1,000 feet. Available in black or blue dial, assembled in the USA. Each watch comes with a leather tool roll made in Texas, a bracelet adjustment tool, and an extra nylon strap at wassonwatch.com.

A Limited Edition Worth Having: Wasson 250th Anniversary Field Watch: With America’s 250th anniversary approaching, Wasson Watch has created a special edition field watch available on a first-come, first-served basis. The full-color US flag anchors the dial, with a commemorative inscription etched on the back. It comes with both a green nylon strap and a red, white, and blue nylon strap — built for the moment, meant to be kept. Two options: a quartz version and a Swiss automatic available in black, blue, or white. 100M water resistant at Wasson Watch.com



The Body Data Dad Didn’t Know Was Needed: RENPHO MorphoScan Nova

RENPHO has built a following of over 18 million users worldwide for one reason: it brings clinical-grade health data home, without the clinical-grade price tag. The MorphoScan Nova is their most advanced offering — an 8-electrode smart body composition scale that goes far beyond weight.

Fifty-plus body metrics available directly through the RENPHO Health app: body fat percentage, visceral fat, metabolic age, bone mass, BMR, water percentage, and more. What sets it apart is segmental analysis — it breaks down fat and muscle distribution per limb, each arm, each leg, and the trunk individually. Trusted by hundreds of clinics, it generates a full printable health report from a single weigh-in.

For the dad who’s working on health, or the one who just wants to know the numbers — this is the gift that gives back every morning at renpho.com.

Rest, Reimagined: RENPHO x Headspace Eyeris Zen Eye Massager: This one is for the Dad who never slows down — and probably should. The Eyeris Zen is a collaboration between RENPHO and Headspace, combining a heated compression eye massager with built-in guided meditations and soundscapes. No phone required. No friction. Three heat levels. Three massage modes. Targets eye strain, puffiness, dryness, and temple tension. Ultra-quiet and lightweight, it works on a couch, a plane, or anywhere else Dad finally decides to stop moving for twenty minutes. Every Eyeris Zen includes a complimentary Headspace Premium trial via QR code at renpho.com.

data.full_text:
Amazon has added a new bedtime feature, called Sleep Studio, to its Echo Kids lineup. It gives children access to a curated library of sleep-focused content, including guided meditations, soundscapes, and stories from Calm, Headspace, and Moshi. The feature is included with Amazon Kids+, a subscription that comes bundled with Echo Dot Kids and Echo Pop Kids. How it works Parents set up sleep schedules and build playlists through the Amazon Kids Parent Dashboard. About 30 minutes before bedtime, the Echo device automatically starts playing the queued content. Kids can also trigger Sleep Studio themselves by asking Alexa, which Amazon says helps build independent sleep habits. Amazon’s Echo Glow can also pair with the feature to add a visual cue through color-coded lighting that signals the start of a sleep window. Content partners and availability The content library draws from three partners. Calm contributes meditation content, lullabies, soundscapes, and sleep stories. Headspace offers wind-down content developed by child psychiatrists and pediatricians. Moshi, the kids-focused audio brand from Mind Candy, adds bedtime stories set in the Moshi Monsters universe. Recommended Videos Amazon says the feature was designed with child sleep research in mind, pointing to National Sleep Foundation data showing nearly half of US children do not get the recommended amount of sleep. Sleep Studio is now available on the Echo Dot Kids, Echo Pop Kids, and any Echo device with an Amazon Kids+ profile enabled. It gives Amazon’s Echo Kids hardware a clearer value proposition in the children’s tech market, where dedicated sleep apps and smart night lights have carved out a loyal audience among parents.

data.title: From Access to Accountability: The Next Chapter in Behavioral Health

data.full_text:
Behavioral health has long represented one of the largest gaps between disease burden and care delivery in the U.S. health system. Nearly one in four American adults — 61.5 million people — experienced a mental health condition in 2024, with of that population also meeting criteria for a substance use disorder. Yet nearly half of those with a mental health condition received no treatment, and fewer than one in five of those needing substance use treatment received it. The economic cost is staggering: $282 billion in annual productivity losses, direct expenditures, and suicide-related costs, and $477.5 billion in avoidable costs attributable to unaddressed mental health inequities, with projections of $14 trillion in cumulative costs through 2040.

COVID-19 forced these gaps into the open. Anxiety and depression prevalence roughly tripled during the pandemic, and within two years, hundreds of digital behavioral health platforms had launched on the premise that technology could close the access gap at scale. Capital flooded in: digital mental health companies raised $4.9 billion in 2021 alone, while behavioral health remained the single most funded clinical indication in digital health every year from 2020 through 2024. The access gap was real, and investor conviction was justified.

This next chapter for digital behavioral health is about moving beyond access – toward accountability, outcomes, and the clinical infrastructure to sustain both. Behavioral health platforms – formed during or shortly after the pandemic – made real progress across several fronts: reducing stigma, dismantling geographic barriers, and reaching underserved populations for the first time. At the same time, utilization growth across the broader sector outpaced meaningful clinical outcomes and population-level ROI remained difficult to verify. The same structural barriers that defined the problem before the pandemic — a worsening provider shortage, fragmented care, and overlap with chronic physical conditions — proved resistant to change at scale.

The Structural Challenges That Remain

The behavioral health system’s persistent challenges are not accidental. They reflect structural misalignments that technology-enabled access alone cannot resolve.

The provider shortage is getting worse, not better. HRSA projects a shortfall of more than 43,000 psychiatrists and 77,000 addiction counselors by 2038. More than 60% of active psychiatrists are aged 55 or older and are likely to retire in the next 10-15 years. No training pipeline adjustment closes this gap on any near-term timeline. Virtual therapy still requires licensed therapists — and the same shortage that constrained in-person care constrained virtual care at scale. The most scalable near-term lever is technology that extends what existing providers can do, not technology that tries to bypass them.

Behavioral health’s overlap with chronic physical conditions compounds the challenge. Individuals with mental illness have two to three times the rate of comorbid conditions including diabetes, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. Comorbid behavioral-physical populations are among the highest per-member cost segment across payers with healthcare costs running 2.8 to 6.2 times higher, and this population accounting for more than 56% of all healthcare costs despite representing only 27% of insured lives. Managing these populations in clinical and administrative silos is both clinically incoherent and economically inefficient.

At the same time, rapid expansion of digital behavioral health during the pandemic exposed structural gaps the sector is still working through. While some platforms built meaningful payer relationships, many entered the market through direct-to-consumer or self-pay channels, limiting their reach within the broader healthcare system. Outcome measurement varied widely: some platforms invested early in measurement-based care, while others tracked enrollment and utilization without systematic outcome data. For employers, the proliferation of point solutions created coordination problems – the average large employer ended up managing several separate behavioral health vendors with limited ability to navigate members across levels of care.

From Access to Accountability

Over the last few years, the market has adjusted accordingly. Today, payers (e.g., health plans) and self-insured employers have begun conditioning contracts on measurement-based care — standardized outcome scales like PHQ-9 and GAD-7, functional improvement data, and documented reductions in downstream medical costs. The commercial model is shifting from per-member-per-month subscription structures toward outcome-tied arrangements: case rate contracts, performance guarantees, and capitated structures that align vendor economics with clinical results rather than enrollment volume.

As a result of the shifting priorities from stakeholders, some first-generation companies have struggled to keep pace. Behavioral health MA jumped 42% in 2025 – the most active year since 2022. We now see three distinct consolidation logics reshaping the market simultaneously: (1) platform aggregation like Spring Health’s acquisition of Alma which combines employer mental health delivery with clinician network infrastructure and payer contracting, (2) health system entry such as UHS’ $835 million acquisition of Talkspace which signals traditional inpatient systems buying virtual delivery channels as a direct response to the workforce shortage, and (3) capability bolt-ons, demonstrated by Noto’s acquisition of Rebound Health, which expanded its specialty therapy platform to include PTSD and Trauma. The fragmented point-solution era is ending. Integrated platforms combining clinical delivery, clinician networks, measurement-based care, and payer contracting are building scale advantages that standalone point solutions cannot replicate.

For health plans, health systems, and employers, the consolidation wave is both an opportunity and a decision point. The platforms building payer relationships and outcomes infrastructure today will have structural contracting advantages that are difficult to overcome later. Partnership decisions made in the next 12 to 24 months will shape which platforms have the network depth and clinical evidence to be viable long-term partners. Two examples illustrate what early, deliberate partnership decisions look like in practice. Evernorth, Cigna’s health services division, partnered with and invested in Octave to build a scalable, measurement-based care infrastructure, growing from 1,000 to 5,000 providers in 18 months and reporting an 84% reduction in depression and anxiety symptoms. Cigna separately partnered with Headspace to extend the care continuum, giving more than 7 million members access to app-based mental health support. Memorial Hermann, facing high-acuity patients arriving in emergency settings with no transitional care options, partnered with Charlie Health to provide virtual intensive outpatient programs, directly targeting the readmission cycle that drives costs. Together, these partnerships reflect a broader shift: health systems and payers are selecting partners not on access metrics alone, but on clinical capacity, care continuum coverage, and measurable outcomes.

Technology Enabling the Next Generation of Behavioral Health Care

The behavioral health workforce crisis is not a temporary imbalance and projected shortages over the next 10 years demonstrate that the supply gap is worsening. Technology is not an efficiency option in this environment — it is a structural necessity.

AI has emerged as the primary lever. Among select behavioral health organizations, AI adoption nearly doubled from 15% in 2024 to 29% in 2025, with clinical documentation and administrative automation leading the way. Ambient documentation tools reduce the time clinicians spend on progress notes, treatment plans, and billing — directly addressing the administrative burden that drives burnout and limits panel size. AI-driven triage and care routing tools match patients to the right level of care faster and more accurately than traditional intake processes, reducing time-to-care and improving patient-provider fit. Continuous outcomes monitoring platforms flag deterioration, medication non-adherence, and engagement risk before they escalate. These capabilities extend what existing providers can do — allowing a constrained workforce to manage more patients without sacrificing clinical quality. For example, Noto, has built the infrastructure layer to transform specialty care at scale: its AI-powered platform supports specialty & condition-specific therapy brands, including NOCD (OCD) and Rebound Health (PTSD and Trauma), by driving payer partnerships, enabling strong enrollment campaigns, and power treatment operations.

Consumer-facing AI is also maturing, but meaningful questions about clinical oversight, safety, and generalizability remain. A 2025 randomized controlled trial of Therabot (Dartmouth) demonstrated clinically significant reductions in depression and anxiety, with effect sizes approaching those of first-line psychotherapy. The researchers emphasized that clinician oversight and validation in larger, more diverse samples are necessary before autonomous deployment at scale. These results are opening a new conversation about coverage pathways for clinically validated AI tools as a workforce multiplier for lower-acuity populations, but it’s critical that a licensed clinician remains accountable for diagnosis and escalation.

The critical distinction the market is drawing today is between supervised AI and autonomous AI. Supervised tools — where a licensed clinician remains accountable for diagnosis, treatment, and escalation — are currently winning payer confidence, navigating FDA’s Software as a Medical Device framework more successfully, and generating the reimbursement traction that autonomous chatbots without clinical oversight have yet to today. For now, the platforms investing in supervised regulatory compliance and clinical validation are building a durable advantage.

The Digital Behavioral Health Market Landscape

Digital behavioral health funding is entering a maturation phase: total funding reached approximately $1 billion in 2025, with average deal size roughly doubling from $12 million to $25 million with capital concentrating within scaled, outcomes-proven platforms rather than early-stage access plays. We organize the market into four segments.

General Outpatient Virtual and Hybrid Care ($335M in 2025 funding). Platforms delivering routine outpatient therapy and psychiatry via telehealth or hybrid models, including provider directories matching patients to in-network clinicians. Competition has shifted from access to clinical model depth: evidence-based therapeutic delivery, prescribing capability, outcomes measurement, and payer contracting sophistication are now table stakes. Notable companies include:

Brightline: Delivers pediatric and young adult mental health care through therapy, psychiatry, and psychological testing via a virtual and in-person hybrid model, with AI embedded across provider productivity, member access, and operations.

Headway: Insurance-based therapist marketplace that simplifies in-network credentialing and billing for independent clinicians, expanding affordable access to outpatient mental health care,

Talkspace: Telehealth platform offering therapy and psychiatry across consumer, employer, and health plan channels, recently acquired by UHS as traditional health systems move into virtual behavioral health delivery,

Condition-Specific and High-Acuity Care ($282M in 2025 funding). Specialized programs targeting defined diagnoses or serious mental illness, combining virtual psychiatry and therapy, peer support, and intensive care coordination. This segment is increasingly defined by the payer contracting depth and outcomes evidence built around discrete conditions. Notable companies include:

NOCD: One of the leading specialty platforms for OCD, delivering live-video Exposure Response & Prevention (ERP) therapy with licensed OCD specialists, 24/7 between-session support through the NOCD app, and coverage across 70+ insurance plans in all 50 states.

Equip: Virtual eating disorder treatment platform delivering family-based care with multidisciplinary clinical teams and payer contracting across commercial and Medicaid plans.

Seven Starling: Virtual perinatal mental health platform delivering therapy, group sessions, and medication management for women navigating fertility, pregnancy, and postpartum.

Consumer Wellness Platforms ($116M in 2025 funding). Direct-to-consumer self-guided apps, conversational agents, and coaching tools operating outside the clinical care setting. This segment faces the most pressure from AI-native entrants, as purpose-built foundation models trained on evidence-based therapeutic frameworks begin to demonstrate clinically meaningful outcomes in RCT settings. Coverage pathway development for clinically validated consumer AI tools is an active area of payer experimentation. Notable companies include:

Headspace: Meditation and mental wellness app now partnering with Cigna to extend coverage to more than 7 million members, with bidirectional referral pathways to in-network clinical care.

Calm: Consumer mindfulness and sleep platform expanding into employer and payer channels as a lower-acuity entry point to the behavioral health care continuum.

Big Health: Digital therapeutics company delivering clinically validated, prescription-grade programs for insomnia and anxiety as an alternative to medication.

Clinical Enablement and Workflow Tools ($242M in 2025 funding). Provider-facing software that surfaces clinical insights, supports measurement-based care, and automates documentation and administrative workflows. This is the highest-growth segment by investment velocity, reflecting the market’s recognition that solving the supply constraint is as economically valuable as building the next consumer-facing platform. Notable companies include:

Eleos Health: Ambient documentation and clinical intelligence platform for behavioral health providers, reducing note-writing time and surfacing outcomes data to support measurement-based care.

Blueprint: Measurement-based care platform that automates outcome scale administration, progress tracking, and treatment planning for outpatient behavioral health practices.

Osmind: AI-native EHR, billing, and care network purpose-built for interventional psychiatry, supporting Spravato, TMS, ketamine, and other emerging modalities across a network of 1,000+ independent practices nationwide.

Perspectives from Key Opinion Leaders

To ground these themes in practitioner and payer experience, we convened a panel of three leaders at the forefront of behavioral health delivery and innovation: Dr. Thomas Insel, former Director of the National Institute of Mental Health and Co-founder and President of Benchmark Health; Corbin Petro, President of Carelon Behavioral Health and the founder of Eleanor Health; and Stephen Smith, Co-founder and CEO of Noto. The conversation reinforced a through-line running across all three perspectives: the behavioral health industry has historically optimized for generalist access, and is now in a phase of optimizing for specialty access and outcomes. Panelists noted that while access expansion was a necessary paradigm during the pandemic and shortly thereafter, the lack of standardized outcome measurement and clinical accountability allowed many companies to scale utilization without connecting people to evidence-based, specialty treatments that drove outcomes. From the payer side, the panel pointed to longitudinal outcome data – connecting clinical improvement to reduced downstream utilization – as the missing link between vendor contracts and demonstrable ROI. And from the delivery side, the panel underscored that quality and scale are not in tension: building outcome infrastructure from the beginning is what enables a specialty platform to grow without sacrificing clinical fidelity. The panel’s collective message aligned with where the market is heading – accountability is not a constraint on behavioral health’s potential. It is the condition for realizing it.

7wire Ventures Predictions

Technology-enabled workforce extension will emerge as the defining investment theme in behavioral health. The provider shortage is structural and will not resolve within any near-to-medium-term horizon. The most scalable solution is enabling existing providers to operate more efficiently and manage larger patient panels. AI-powered documentation, triage automation, and outcomes tracking tools are reducing the administrative burden that drives burnout and limits panel size — directly expanding effective clinical capacity without requiring new provider supply. Expect dedicated investment in behavioral health provider enablement as a distinct category, separate from care delivery platforms, as the market recognizes that solving the supply constraint is as economically valuable as building the next consumer application. Consumer-facing AI tools with clinical validation will begin to find coverage pathways as payers recognize their potential as a workforce multiplier for lower-acuity populations. Outcomes data will become the primary basis for payer and employer contract decisions — reshaping which companies win. Platforms with peer-reviewed ROI and payer network depth will continue to consolidate market share as utilization-focused platforms restructure or exit. Measurement-based care will shift from a differentiator to a baseline requirement: platforms that cannot generate standardized outcome data will be excluded from value-based contracts across both payer and employer channels. For health plans, the shift toward outcomes-tied contracting will also drive consolidation of vendor relationships — from fragmented point solutions toward fewer, more accountable platform partners. Behavioral health integration into whole-person care models will become economically mandatory, not clinically aspirational. As Medicare Advantage penetration grows and value-based contracts place providers at financial risk for total cost of care, untreated behavioral health comorbidities become directly attributable to medical spend. The Collaborative Care Model — embedding behavioral health into primary care through structured screening, care management, and psychiatric consultation — will see broader adoption as reimbursement pathways mature and workflow integration barriers decrease. Platforms that can manage behavioral health alongside metabolic and chronic physical conditions will be preferentially contracted as the cardio-kidney-metabolic framework gains commercial traction.Behavioral health is not a niche clinical category. It is among the fastest-growing cost drivers in American healthcare, deeply entangled with every chronic condition that payers and health systems struggle to manage. The first wave of digital innovation proved that technology could expand access. The next wave will prove that technology can drive accountability — that people get better, that costs come down, and that the platforms delivering those outcomes can be measured, contracted, and trusted. At 7wire Ventures, we are closely tracking the companies building the infrastructure for that accountability era, and we believe the next generation of behavioral health platforms will be defined not by how many people they can enroll, but by the outcomes they can demonstrate and the system relationships they have earned.
