data.title: The best spiritual and mindfulness apps for meditation, astrology, breathwork and manifestation
data.ai_summary: This article is a curated buyer's guide reviewing seven spiritual, mindfulness and wellness apps available for UK users, including Nebula, Insight Timer, Headspace, Breathwrk, Sadhguru, SimpleMind, and Law of Attraction Toolbox. The guide evaluates each app based on features, pricing models, free content availability, platform availability, and suitability for different user needs such as meditation, astrology, breathwork, and manifestation practices. The article aims to help readers identify which app best suits their wellness goals, noting that free options like Insight Timer and Sadhguru offer substantial content without subscription costs.
data.author: Victoria Woollaston-Webber

industries.name: Meditation Apps, Digital Courses & Online Communities

data.full_text:
We’ve handpicked seven of the best spiritual, mindfulness and psychic apps worth adding to your daily routine in the UK

Nebula combines astrology, psychic readings, tarot and dream analysis in one place. Insight Timer is a free mindfulness app with thousands of guided meditations, breathwork sessions and sleep tools. Headspace is mindfulness for beginners or anyone who wants a structured, guided introduction to meditation. If breathwork is your focus, Breathwrk (now owned by Peleton) offers sessions by mood and energy level. Sadhguru is for anyone exploring yoga philosophy alongside meditation and guided practice. SimpleMind works well for journalling, intention-mapping and visual self-reflection. Law of Attraction Toolbox is best for manifestation-focused routines and intention-setting.

Wellness apps have been around long enough now that most of us will have downloaded at least one before likely having forgotten about them.

In our experience, the ones that actually stick tend to do something specific really well, whether that’s guided breathwork to take the edge off a stressful day, a daily astrology reading that gives you something to think about, or a meditation practice that’s short enough to fit into your morning.

This guide covers seven of the best spiritual, mindfulness and psychic apps available in the UK right now.

We’ve looked at everything from free meditation tools to paid platforms offering live psychic readings, so there’s something here regardless of where you’re starting from or what you’re looking for.

We’ve also addressed the questions that come up most often – whether these apps are worth paying for, how accurate psychic apps really are, and which ones are worth trying if you’ve never used anything like this before.

Best spiritual apps at a glance

Not sure where to start? Here’s a quick summary of what each app does best:

Comparing mindfulness and spiritual apps

Here’s a quick comparison of all seven apps across the most important factors:

App Best for Free version iPhone Android Nebula Astrology and psychic guidance Partial ✓ ✓ Insight Timer Meditation and mindfulness ✓ ✓ ✓ Headspace Beginners Partial ✓ ✓ Breathwrk Breathwork Partial ✓ ✓ Sadhguru Yoga and spirituality ✓ ✓ ✓ SimpleMind Journalling and intention-mapping ✓ ✓ ✓ Law of Attraction Toolbox Manifestation Partial ✓ ✓

Nebula – Best for astrology, psychic readings and spiritual guidance

Image credit: Nebula Who it’s best for: Anyone curious about astrology, birth charts, tarot or psychic guidance who wants access to a range of vetted advisors in one place.

Anyone curious about astrology, birth charts, tarot or psychic guidance who wants access to a range of vetted advisors in one place. Pricing: Free to download; live readings charged per minute (rates vary by advisor). Introductory offers available for new users.

Free to download; live readings charged per minute (rates vary by advisor). Introductory offers available for new users. What we like: The breadth of content, the advisor rating system, and the self-discovery tools that are genuinely useful without booking a reading. It works well as an online wellness platform beyond just the psychic element.

The breadth of content, the advisor rating system, and the self-discovery tools that are genuinely useful without booking a reading. It works well as an online wellness platform beyond just the psychic element. What could be better: The per-minute pricing model means you just need to be mindful (excuse the pun) of costs.

The per-minute pricing model means you just need to be mindful (excuse the pun) of costs. Platforms: iOS, Android, web

Nebula is a spiritual guidance platform that brings together astrology, tarot, psychic readings and dream analysis in one app. If you’ve ever found yourself reading your horoscope in one tab, looking up tarot card meanings in another and Googling what a dream about your ex actually means, Nebula is essentially designed to stop that tab spiral.

The platform connects you with individual advisors who have their own profiles, ratings, specialties and reviews. You can filter by topic – love, career, family, life path – and choose someone whose approach resonates with you, whether that’s astrology-based readings, tarot, or more intuition-led psychic guidance. There are also self-discovery tools built in, including birth chart generators, rising sign calculators and compatibility tools, which are useful even if you never book a paid reading.

The app itself is free to download, and there’s enough free content – daily horoscopes, educational articles, self-discovery tools – to get a feel for whether it’s the kind of thing you’d use regularly.You can also, optionally, pay for live readings and Nebula uses a per-minute model with the prices per advisor shown up front. There are introductory offers for new users, which makes it a reasonable way to test the platform without a significant upfront commitment.

The advisor vetting process is more transparent than many competitors, and the range of specialties means you’re not limited to one type of reading. If you’re curious about what a psychic reading app actually involves, or you want a single place for all things astrology, Nebula is worth a look – just keep an eye on your session time.

Insight Timer – Best free mindfulness and meditation app

Image credit: Insight Timer

Who it’s best for: Anyone who wants a free, broad and flexible mindfulness app without being pushed towards a specific practice or tradition.

Anyone who wants a free, broad and flexible mindfulness app without being pushed towards a specific practice or tradition. What we like: The depth of the free library, the lack of pressure to subscribe, and the variety of content styles.

The depth of the free library, the lack of pressure to subscribe, and the variety of content styles. What could be better: The sheer amount of content can feel overwhelming at first. It’s worth using the search filters rather than scrolling through everything.

The sheer amount of content can feel overwhelming at first. It’s worth using the search filters rather than scrolling through everything. Pricing: Free with optional paid subscription for offline access and premium courses.

Free with optional paid subscription for offline access and premium courses. Platforms: iOS, Android

Insight Timer has one of the largest free meditation libraries of any app currently available, which immediately puts it ahead of most of the competition. The free tier isn’t a teaser – it gives you access to thousands of guided meditations, breathwork sessions, yoga nidra recordings, sleep music, talks and short courses. You’d need to use it for a very long time before running out of content without spending anything.

The app spans a wide range of traditions and teaching styles, so it doesn’t push a particular approach. You can find everything from body scan meditations and Vipassana-style techniques to sound baths, Reiki sessions and sleep stories. There’s a timer function if you prefer unguided practice – you can set bells at intervals, choose ambient sounds, and track your sitting time over weeks and months.

For those who want more structure, there are teacher-led courses and live events available, though some of these sit behind a paid subscription. The paid tier (Insight Timer Plus) also unlocks offline listening and deeper course content. That said, the free version is substantial enough that plenty of people never feel the need to upgrade.

Mood tracking and journalling options are also built in, which helps if you’re trying to build consistency and want to notice patterns in how you’re feeling over time. It’s particularly good if you’re new to meditation and not sure what style suits you – the sheer range of content means you can explore without committing to one teacher or method. It’s also a solid pairing for anyone already using simple self-care rituals who wants to add something more intentional to their day.

3. Sadhguru – Best for yogic spirituality and philosophy

Image credit: Sadhguru App Who it’s best for: Anyone drawn to yogic philosophy, Isha teachings, or wanting to combine breathwork and meditation with a more structured spiritual framework.

Anyone drawn to yogic philosophy, Isha teachings, or wanting to combine breathwork and meditation with a more structured spiritual framework. What we like: The depth of content, the genuinely free access to most of it, and the breadth of formats from short daily content to longer talks.

The depth of content, the genuinely free access to most of it, and the breadth of formats from short daily content to longer talks. What could be better: It’s very specific to the Sadhguru and Isha tradition. If you’re not interested in that lineage, other apps will serve you better.

It’s very specific to the Sadhguru and Isha tradition. If you’re not interested in that lineage, other apps will serve you better. Pricing: Free

Free Platforms: iOS, Android

The Sadhguru app is built around the teachings and practices of Sadhguru, an Indian yogi and founder of Isha Foundation. It’s not a general meditation app – it’s specifically rooted in yogic philosophy and Isha Yoga practices, so it’s best suited to people who are interested in that tradition rather than looking for something more eclectic.

Content includes daily quotes, short wisdom videos, audio talks, podcasts, longer-form articles and guided practices. The Sounds of Isha section covers chants and music from the Isha community, which some people find useful as background for practice or simply for winding down. The app also makes it easy to find and register for Isha Yoga programmes if you want to take things further in person.

Practices are organised around specific goals – health, balance, focus and inner growth – which makes it easier to know what to start with depending on what you’re looking to work on. Content is available in multiple languages, which is a practical consideration if English isn’t your first language or if you’re sharing the app with family members.

It’s free to download and most content is available without a subscription, which is a meaningful difference from many wellness apps that put the most useful material behind a paywall. If you’ve been curious about yoga as a spiritual practice rather than just a fitness class, this is a good place to start exploring without any financial commitment.

Breathwrk – Best breathwork app for stress and energy

Image credit: Breathwrk

Who it’s best for: Anyone who wants a focused, structured breathwork practice rather than a general meditation or wellness app.

Anyone who wants a focused, structured breathwork practice rather than a general meditation or wellness app. What we like: The goal-based session structure, offline functionality, and the fact that it makes breathwork genuinely easy to follow.

The goal-based session structure, offline functionality, and the fact that it makes breathwork genuinely easy to follow. What could be better: It’s narrowly focused, so it’s not the right choice if you’re looking for meditation or journalling tools alongside breathwork.

It’s narrowly focused, so it’s not the right choice if you’re looking for meditation or journalling tools alongside breathwork. Pricing: Free with optional premium subscription.

Free with optional premium subscription. Platforms: iOS, Android

Breathwrk does one thing and does it well: it guides you through breathing exercises. That might sound simple, but the app is more useful than trying to follow breathing patterns from a YouTube video or a text description because the visual guides actually pace you through the inhale, hold, and exhale phases in real time.

Sessions are organised by what you’re trying to achieve – calming down, boosting energy, improving sleep, sharpening focus, or recovering after exercise. That makes it practical in a way that some wellness apps aren’t. You’re not scrolling through a library trying to find something appropriate; you just tell the app what you need and it gives you a relevant session. This makes it a useful tool alongside an evening routine or as a stress management tool during the day.

There are habit-tracking features and streaks to help with consistency, as well as live classes with professional coaches for those who want more accountability. The app works offline, which matters if you want to use it during travel, on a flight, or in situations where you don’t have a reliable connection.

Some of the more advanced sessions and features sit behind a paid subscription, but there’s enough in the free tier to get a genuine sense of whether the approach works for you before committing. Breathwork has good evidence behind it for stress reduction and sleep, so if that’s your primary concern, this is worth trying before defaulting to a broader meditation app.

Headspace – Best mindfulness app for beginners

Image credit: Headspace

Who it’s best for: Beginners who want a structured, well-designed introduction to mindfulness and meditation.

Beginners who want a structured, well-designed introduction to mindfulness and meditation. What we like: The beginner-friendly progression, the strong sleep content, and the overall quality of the guided sessions.

The beginner-friendly progression, the strong sleep content, and the overall quality of the guided sessions. What could be better: The subscription price is higher than some alternatives, and the free tier is fairly limited.

The subscription price is higher than some alternatives, and the free tier is fairly limited. Pricing: Subscription-based (free trial available).

Subscription-based (free trial available). Platforms: iOS, Android

Headspace is one of the most recognisable names in mindfulness apps, and it’s still one of the better starting points for anyone who’s never tried a structured meditation practice before. The sessions are short – most of the beginner content runs between five and fifteen minutes – and they build progressively so you’re not thrown into something that assumes prior experience.

The app covers stress management, sleep, focus, movement, and general mindfulness, with different programmes for different goals. The sleep content is particularly strong – there are sleep podcasts, wind-down exercises and audio-based bedtime stories designed to help you switch off rather than lie there replaying your day. The interface is well-designed and the guided sessions feel calm rather than overly enthusiastic, which makes a difference when you’re actually trying to relax.

Headspace operates on a subscription model, which is the main drawback. The free content is limited compared to what Insight Timer offers for free, so if cost is a factor, Insight Timer is worth considering first. That said, Headspace’s structure and design are noticeably more polished, and for some people that makes them more likely to actually use it consistently. It’s NHS-recommended too.

If you’ve tried meditation before and found it difficult to know where to start, or if you’ve downloaded an app and not used it past the first week, Headspace’s guided progression is specifically designed to address that. The daily suggestions and short resets make it easier to maintain a habit even on days when you don’t have much time or motivation. It pairs well with other self-care rituals that support your mental wellbeing.

Law of Attraction Toolbox – Best for manifestation and intention-setting

Image credit: The Law of Attraction Toolbox

Who it’s best for: Anyone interested in manifestation, intention-setting or building a more structured daily gratitude and mindset practice.

Anyone interested in manifestation, intention-setting or building a more structured daily gratitude and mindset practice. What we like: The practical tools that translate vague goals into daily habits, and the journalling features that encourage consistency.

The practical tools that translate vague goals into daily habits, and the journalling features that encourage consistency. What could be better: If you’re deeply sceptical of the manifestation framework, there are more neutral mindfulness apps that cover similar habits without the Law of Attraction branding.

If you’re deeply sceptical of the manifestation framework, there are more neutral mindfulness apps that cover similar habits without the Law of Attraction branding. Pricing: Free with in-app purchases.

Free with in-app purchases. Platforms: iOS, Android

Manifestation as a concept has attracted a fair amount of eye-rolling over the years but the Law of Attraction Toolbox is less about magical thinking and more about building structured habits around intention-setting, gratitude and mindset – which are grounded enough to be useful even if you’re not fully bought into the philosophy.

The app provides practical tools rather than just content to consume. There’s a focus wheel designed to redirect your thinking towards a desired outcome, scripting exercises where you write out your goals as if they’ve already happened, future pacing tools, a gratitude journal and visualisation timers. The idea is that you pick an intention and engage with it actively through daily practice rather than just thinking about it vaguely.

Whether you believe in the law of attraction or not, the underlying behaviours the app encourages – journalling, daily gratitude, visualisation, consistent reflection – are associated with improved wellbeing. It’s a structured way of building those habits if you struggle to maintain them through sheer willpower. The app works best when used regularly and with a specific intention rather than browsing between features without focus.

SimpleMind – Best for journalling and intention-mapping

Image credit: SimpleMind Who it’s best for: Visual thinkers who want a flexible tool for self-reflection, goal-mapping, ritual planning or working through recurring thoughts and patterns.

Free with optional premium version. Platforms: iOS, Android, web

SimpleMind is a mind-mapping app, not a spiritual app in the traditional sense. But for anyone who finds linear journalling frustrating or who thinks better in visual structures, it’s one of the more useful tools for self-reflection, intention-mapping and organising your thoughts around spiritual practice or personal growth.

The app lets you create free-form mind maps where you can connect ideas, track recurring thoughts, plan rituals, map out goals, or work through values and decisions visually. It’s particularly useful for people who feel stuck when faced with a blank page – the branching structure makes it easier to start somewhere without committing to a linear narrative. Dream notes, manifestation plans and spiritual routines all work well in this format.

There are auto-layout options for those who want a cleaner visual structure, an autofocus mode that reduces clutter, and export options so you can save or share your maps. You can add notes, images, icons and colour coding to make maps more personal and easier to navigate over time.

It’s one of the more overlooked tools in this space, partly because it doesn’t market itself as a wellness app. But for visual thinkers who want something more structured than a notebook and less prescriptive than a guided journalling app, it fills a gap that most dedicated spiritual apps don’t address.

Are spiritual and mindfulness apps worth it?

The short answer is that it depends on what you do with them.

If you’re someone who benefits from structure, accountability, or simply having good content readily available when you need it, the right app can make a difference to how you manage stress, sleep and general wellbeing.

The research on mindfulness and breathwork is reasonably solid – there’s good evidence that regular practice reduces perceived stress and improves sleep quality over time. Whether you need an app for that or not is personal. Some people find the structure helpful; others do better with books, classes or just sitting quietly for ten minutes without prompts.

For psychic and astrology apps, while there’s no empirical science they can offer a structured framework for reflection, a way to think about current situations from a different angle, and – for some people – a degree of comfort or clarity they find useful.

If cost is a concern, there are enough good free options here – Insight Timer and Sadhguru in particular – that you don’t need to spend anything to find out whether this kind of tool works for you but like with most things, to get the biggest benefits you often have to pay.

Spiritual and mindfulness apps: FAQs

Image credit: iStock

What are spiritual apps?

Spiritual apps are mobile platforms designed to support practices like meditation, astrology, tarot, breathwork, journalling, manifestation and psychic guidance. They vary widely in focus – some are purely meditation tools, others connect you with live advisors for readings, and some are self-reflection tools that don’t fit neatly into any one category. The term covers a broad range of approaches, so the best one for you depends on what you’re actually looking for.

What is the best spiritual app in the UK?

Nebula is the most comprehensive option if you want astrology, psychic readings and spiritual guidance in one place. For meditation and mindfulness, Insight Timer is the strongest free option and Headspace is the best choice for beginners who want a structured programme. The best mindfulness app depends on what you’re looking for.

Are there free spiritual apps?

Yes. Insight Timer and Sadhguru are both free with substantial content available without a subscription. Headspace, Breathwrk and Nebula all offer partial free access with some content or features gated behind a paid tier. If you want to try before spending money, Insight Timer is the most generous starting point.

Which app is best for meditation?

Insight Timer has the largest free meditation library of any app currently available. Headspace is better if you want a more guided, structured approach – it builds progressively and is particularly helpful if you’re new to meditation and not sure how to begin. For meditation rooted in yoga philosophy, Sadhguru is worth considering.

Which mindfulness app is best for beginners?

Headspace is designed specifically with beginners in mind. It starts simple, builds progressively, and the sessions are short enough to fit into a day without feeling like a significant commitment. It’s also NHS-recommended, which matters if you’re using it for stress or anxiety management. Insight Timer is a close second if cost is a factor, since the free tier gives you access to beginner-friendly content without any subscription.

Are mindfulness apps worth paying for?

It depends on whether you’ll actually use them consistently. If you’re the kind of person who benefits from structure and finds free apps less motivating, a paid subscription might be worth it for accountability alone. If you’re not sure, start with a free option like Insight Timer and see whether you use it regularly before spending money. Most paid apps also offer free trials, so there’s no need to commit without testing first.

Are psychic apps real?

The advisors on psychic apps are real people with genuine experience in whatever they offer – whether that’s astrology, tarot, numerology, or intuitive readings. Whether psychic ability itself is real is a much bigger question and we’re not here to judge anyone’s beliefs. What psychic apps can offer is a structured conversation with someone who takes these traditions seriously, a framework for thinking about your situation, and sometimes a useful outside perspective. Whether that has value to you is personal.

Are psychic apps legitimate?

The better-known platforms like Nebula do vet their advisors and have review systems in place, which provides more accountability than a random search result. Look for platforms that show advisor ratings and reviews, and be cautious of anyone who makes very specific predictions or asks for additional payments mid-session.

How accurate are psychic apps?

There’s no scientific standard by which psychic accuracy can be measured, so this is difficult to answer. What most people find useful about psychic readings – whether in person or via an app – is less about specific predictions and more about the reflective process of talking through a situation with someone who approaches it differently.

How we chose the best spiritual apps

There’s no shortage of wellness apps to choose from, which makes picking the right one harder, not easier. These are the criteria we used to narrow things down:

data.ai_summary: Digital health has become one of the fastest-growing sectors for business investment heading into 2026, as healthcare organizations shift from experimental apps to infrastructure-level systems like AI documentation tools, remote patient monitoring, and workflow automation. Major drivers include rising administrative costs (McKinsey estimates ~25% of U.S. healthcare spending), worsening clinical staff shortages, and surging demand for mental health services. Companies like Teladoc Health, Headspace Health, Spring Health, and Microsoft-backed Nuance Communications are actively expanding enterprise contracts in this environment, with cybersecurity spending also accelerating following high-profile attacks like the 2024 Change Healthcare breach.

data.full_text:
Why Digital Health Is Becoming One of the Fastest-Growing Sectors for Business Investment in 2026

For years, healthcare was considered one of the slowest industries to modernize. Hospitals still relied on fax machines. Patient records were trapped inside disconnected systems. Booking an appointment often felt harder than ordering a mortgage online. That picture is changing fast. Healthcare providers, insurers, employers, and investors are now pouring money into digital platforms because the economics are hard to ignore. Administrative costs remain enormous, clinical staff shortages are worsening, and patient demand keeps climbing. The old operating model is struggling under its own weight. This is why digital health has become one of the most active areas for business investment heading into 2026. Large healthcare systems are no longer treating software as a side purchase managed by IT departments. Digital infrastructure is becoming part of the core operational strategy. Companies building remote care platforms, AI-assisted clinical tools, and behavioral health systems are now competing for the same investment dollars that previously flowed into fintech and enterprise SaaS. A major driver is mental healthcare. Demand has outpaced provider capacity in the U.S., the U.K., and much of Europe for years. Many healthcare organizations are turning to specialized platforms and working with experienced teams in mental health app development, like SysGears to build scalable products that can handle teletherapy, patient engagement, secure communications, and compliance requirements at enterprise scale. The shift is visible across the market. In early 2026, companies like Teladoc Health, Headspace Health, and Spring Health continue expanding enterprise healthcare contracts even as broader tech funding remains selective. That matters because healthcare buyers are notoriously cautious. Hospitals do not replace systems quickly. Insurers do not approve new vendors casually. If spending is accelerating in this environment, it usually signals a structural change rather than a temporary trend. Hospitals are buying infrastructure now, not experimental apps A few years ago, digital health investment often centered on consumer wellness apps chasing rapid user growth. Many of those companies struggled once acquisition costs rose, and pandemic demand cooled. The market looks different now. Healthcare organizations are spending on infrastructure-level systems tied directly to operations: remote patient monitoring, clinical workflow automation, digital intake, AI documentation tools, and interoperability platforms. Some of the strongest growth is happening in products that reduce administrative overhead. According to estimates from McKinsey & Company, administrative spending accounts for roughly 25% of total U.S. healthcare costs. Even modest efficiency gains can translate into billions in savings. That explains the surge in adoption around AI medical scribes and workflow automation platforms. Nuance Communications, now part of Microsoft, continues expanding its Dragon Ambient eXperience platform, which automatically generates clinical notes during patient visits. Physicians like the time savings. Hospital executives like the staffing math behind it. Still, most healthcare systems see the tradeoff as worthwhile because clinician burnout has become a financial problem, not just a workplace issue. Mental healthcare became impossible to ignore Behavioral healthcare used to sit on the edge of healthcare technology discussions. That is no longer true. In the U.S., demand for therapy and psychiatric care surged after the pandemic and never fully stabilized. Employers now treat mental health support as part of their workforce retention strategy. Universities are expanding virtual counseling programs because in-person capacity cannot keep up. Insurers increasingly reimburse digital behavioral care because untreated mental health conditions drive higher downstream medical costs. This has created a strong market for mental health software focused on long-term engagement rather than one-time consultations. Mental health platforms operate in highly sensitive environments where privacy failures can permanently damage trust. A meditation app leaking user preferences is embarrassing. A therapy platform exposing patient records is catastrophic. That complexity is pushing healthcare companies toward experienced engineering teams rather than general-purpose app vendors. Choosing a software development partner with healthcare-specific expertise has become a risk management decision as much as a technical one. AI hype is everywhere, but healthcare buyers are getting skeptical Artificial intelligence dominates healthcare conferences in 2026. Nearly every vendor claims to have AI capabilities. Investors are still funding the category aggressively. Healthcare executives, though, have become more cautious. Hospitals learned from earlier waves of healthcare technology adoption that flashy demos rarely reflect operational reality. Integration problems, poor data quality, and compliance gaps can turn promising tools into expensive distractions. Scheduling optimization is one example. Predictive no-show models are helping providers reduce empty appointment slots. Revenue cycle tools are identifying insurance claim issues earlier. AI-assisted imaging platforms are helping radiologists prioritize urgent cases faster. These are practical systems tied directly to cost reduction or throughput improvement. The market has become far less forgiving toward companies selling vague “AI-powered healthcare ecosystems” without clinical validation or clear deployment models. That shift is healthy for the industry. Remote care is becoming standard in several specialties Telehealth usage dropped from its pandemic peak, but it did not disappear. Instead, it settled into areas where virtual care genuinely makes operational sense. That distinction matters because investors are becoming more disciplined about where digital health platforms can realistically scale. Cybersecurity is now part of healthcare spending strategy Healthcare remains one of the most targeted industries for ransomware attacks. Patient records are valuable. Hospital downtime is expensive. Many provider systems still run on outdated infrastructure that was never designed for modern threat environments. In 2024, the cyberattack on Change Healthcare disrupted pharmacy operations, insurance claims, and payment processing across the U.S. healthcare system. The fallout continued for months. Incidents like that changed boardroom conversations. Healthcare organizations are increasing spending on cloud security, identity management, encryption, and infrastructure resilience because outages now carry operational and regulatory consequences far beyond IT departments. Healthcare systems are trying to reduce long-term operational risk while modernizing fragmented infrastructure that should have been replaced years ago. The companies benefiting most in 2026 are not necessarily the loudest startups or the most consumer-visible brands. Many are enterprise-focused vendors solving deeply unglamorous problems inside healthcare operations. That is where the money is moving now. Article received via email

sleep Headspace vs BetterSleep: Which App Should You Pick? Written by Chris Barry May 29, 2026 • 5 min read

Content summary Headspace and BetterSleep solve different problems. Headspace is a meditation app with sleep content built on a mindfulness framework — best if you want to build a meditation practice and improve sleep along the way. BetterSleep is a sleep-first app with a customizable sound mixer, sleep stories, and bedtime routines — best if your goal is falling asleep faster. Headspace costs $69.99/year; BetterSleep costs $59.99/year with a $249 lifetime option. Try BetterSleep for FREEDownload the BetterSleep App

Millions of people now use sleep and meditation apps to help with stress, anxiety, insomnia, and nighttime routines. But once you narrow the options down to Headspace and BetterSleep, the comparison becomes surprisingly confusing. The two apps overlap just enough to look similar at first glance, even though they’re actually built for very different kinds of users. Headspace and BetterSleep solve different problems. Headspace is a meditation app with sleep content built on a mindfulness framework — best if you want to build a meditation practice and improve sleep as a byproduct. BetterSleep is a sleep app built around customizable soundscapes, sleep stories, and tracking tools — best if your primary goal is falling asleep faster. Headspace costs $69.99/year; BetterSleep costs $59.99/year with a lifetime option available. Most comparison articles treat Headspace and BetterSleep as direct competitors, but they’re actually designed around different priorities. People comparing sleep apps also tend to look at Calm before deciding which platform fits them best. Headspace started as a meditation platform and gradually expanded into sleep content. BetterSleep took the opposite approach: it was built first as a sleep-focused app, then later added meditation and mindfulness features around that core experience. If your biggest problem is stress, anxious thinking, or difficulty slowing down at night, Headspace has the stronger meditation framework and a more structured sleep program. But if your priorities are more practical — falling asleep faster, managing environmental noise, building better bedtime routines, or having more control over your nighttime audio environment — BetterSleep is much more purpose-built. Which App Makes More Sense for You? Pick BetterSleep if your main goal is falling asleep more easily and building a better nighttime routine. The app is designed around what people actually do at bedtime: choose a sound, start a story, follow a wind-down routine, check their sleep patterns, or adjust the room’s audio environment until it feels right. The sound mixer is the clearest example of that sleep-first approach. You can combine rain, brown noise, ocean sounds, fan noise, soft piano, binaural beats, or solfeggio frequencies into mixes that match how you fall asleep on a given night. Some nights you might want guided narration. Some nights you just want steady background sound. Some nights you want almost no stimulation at all except a low ambient tone underneath the room noise. That’s where BetterSleep feels different from a meditation-first app. Sleep stories, soundscapes, bedtime routines, snore detection, and sleep tracking are positioned as core features rather than secondary additions attached to a meditation platform. BetterSleep approaches sleep tracking differently than dedicated wearable ecosystems. Its microphone-based tracking is designed more for general nightly insights and habit awareness than detailed sleep-stage analysis, and that level of feedback is enough for most people to notice patterns and improve their routines over time. Pick Headspace if your biggest issue is mental overstimulation at night. The meditation library is deeper, the structured courses are stronger, and the app does a better job of helping users build a long-term mindfulness practice instead of simply helping them relax at bedtime. Its guided programs feel slightly more cohesive, and its newer CBT-I-based sleep program adds real clinical credibility to the platform. Headspace feels more guided and structured. BetterSleep gives you more control and customization. If you want a meditation app that also improves sleep, Headspace is probably the stronger choice. If you want a sleep app that also includes meditation tools, BetterSleep makes more sense for most people. What Each App Is Actually Built For Both offer sleep content, guided meditations, bedtime audio, and calming wellness features. But after a few days of actually using them, the difference becomes obvious. Headspace feels like a meditation platform that expanded outward into stress reduction, sleep support, focus tools, and mindfulness routines. Even its sleep content revolves around calming the mind first. The app assumes that better sleep starts with calming mental overstimulation and anxiety. If your sleep problems are closely tied to racing thoughts, chronic stress, or difficulty mentally disengaging at night, Headspace’s structure can feel reassuring. The app guides you step-by-step instead of asking you to build your own experience from scratch. BetterSleep approaches the problem from the opposite direction. The app focuses much more heavily on the physical experience of falling asleep: sound environment, bedtime routines, ambient audio, sleep stories, and nightly sleep habits. Meditation exists inside the platform, but it doesn’t dominate the experience in the same way it does with Headspace. With Headspace, you often feel like you’re entering a guided wellness program, which doesn’t necessarily jibe with everybody. With BetterSleep, you feel like you’re building a sleep environment tailored to how your brain and body relax at night. The BetterSleep sound mixer is a good example of this. Instead of simply pressing play on a single track, you can layer sounds together and adjust them individually: rain underneath brown noise, ocean waves plus soft piano, or wind with a low ambient hum underneath everything else. And while Headspace does include sleepcasts and ambient audio, the experience is more curated and less flexible overall. Some people prefer that simplicity. Others eventually want more control over the sounds they fall asleep to. Sleep Features Compared, Feature by Feature Sleep Stories and Sleepcasts The bedtime audio feels noticeably different once you spend time with each app’s library. BetterSleep offers a larger overall range of sleep stories and styles. That variety matters because more people are now using bedtime storytelling as a way to mentally disengage before sleep instead of simply masking background noise. You’ll find nature journeys, fantasy environments, mystery stories, travel scenarios, calming documentaries, children’s bedtime stories, and slower narration tracks designed for people who dislike overly theatrical voice acting. There’s also more tonal variety. Some narrators are very restrained and almost whisper-like. Others are more animated and conversational. Some stories barely have a plot at all and are really just designed to help you drift off. Headspace’s Sleepcasts are generally more polished. The production quality is consistently strong, and the app blends narration with ambient sound very well. Most Sleepcasts feel carefully paced, with just enough descriptive detail to occupy your attention without keeping your brain too alert. In practice, Headspace’s sleep content might feel more polished, but BetterSleep’s library is broader and more customizable. If you want tighter production and a more guided experience, Headspace probably wins this category. If you want variety and more freedom to find the kind of nighttime audio your brain responds to, BetterSleep has the advantage. Soundscapes and the Sound Mixer This is where BetterSleep really separates itself. The BetterSleep sound mixer is one of the app’s defining tools, and for some people it becomes the main reason they keep the subscription long term. The app gives you far more control over your nighttime audio environment than most competitors, especially once you start experimenting with layered sound combinations and custom mixes. You can layer more than 200 sounds together and control each element independently. Rain, brown noise, thunderstorms, waterfalls, fan sounds, distant trains, crackling fireplaces, low ambient drones, soft piano, birds, wind, café ambience — almost every category of sleep audio is represented somewhere inside the library. The app also includes binaural beats and solfeggio frequencies, which some users incorporate into relaxation routines. Research on those specific audio approaches remains mixed, but many people still find them calming as part of a bedtime ritual. Instead of encouraging users to build custom sound environments, the app leans more heavily into guided listening experiences. Ambient sound exists, but customization is much more limited overall. For some users, that simplicity is a strength. But if personalized sound design is important to you — especially if background sound is a major part of how you fall asleep — BetterSleep offers far more flexibility. Sleep Tracking and Snore Detection Headspace doesn’t really function as a sleep tracking app. It tracks meditation consistency and mindfulness activity, but it doesn’t meaningfully track sleep duration, snoring, or overnight sleep behavior. BetterSleep includes microphone-based sleep tracking and snore detection designed to give users a general sense of their nighttime patterns. You can review estimated sleep duration, listen to recorded snoring samples, and monitor changes in nighttime habits over time. Its tracking tools are designed more around habit awareness and nightly patterns than highly detailed biometric analysis. Reviews of consumer sleep apps have found that many are more useful for tracking habits and routines than for delivering precise sleep-stage analysis. Most people mainly want to know whether they slept poorly, woke frequently, snored heavily, or maintained a consistent routine. CBT-I Programs and Structured Sleep Support This is where Headspace regains some ground. Headspace’s newer “Finding Your Best Sleep” program adds something many sleep-focused apps still lack: a more structured behavioral framework based partly around CBT-I principles. CBT-I remains one of the most evidence-supported non-pharmaceutical approaches for chronic insomnia. The program is still designed for mainstream app users rather than clinical treatment, but it gives Headspace more credibility in the structured sleep-improvement category than some might realize. BetterSleep approaches sleep in a less clinical way overall. Instead of guiding users through structured behavioral frameworks, the app focuses more heavily on relaxation, bedtime consistency, environmental control, calming audio, and nightly routines. For users whose sleep struggles are more environmental or habit-based than deeply cognitive, that can feel much more approachable. Meditation Features Compared Meditation is still Headspace’s clearest advantage over BetterSleep. It’s also the foundation the app was built on, and after years of refining the platform, it still feels more complete as a long-term mindfulness app. The guided meditation library is larger, more structured, and generally easier to navigate if meditation itself is your primary goal. (Readers interested in how mindfulness techniques may affect sleep quality can explore BetterSleep’s guide to the science of sleep meditation for a deeper breakdown of the research.) There are courses for stress, anxiety, focus, burnout, grief, productivity, emotional regulation, and sleep, along with shorter standalone sessions for specific moods or situations. Instead of feeling like isolated audio tracks, many Headspace programs feel intentionally progressive, with techniques and ideas layered gradually over time. For users trying to establish an actual meditation habit — not just relax before bed — that structure matters. With that said, BetterSleep includes guided meditations too, and they’ll be more than enough for people who mainly want help winding down at night. Readers looking for additional guided sleep meditations from BetterSleep can also explore the company’s broader meditation recommendations and sleep-focused sessions. Meditation inside BetterSleep is more integrated into a broader sleep-and-relaxation toolkit rather than functioning as the platform’s central identity. Sessions tend to be shorter, more relaxation-focused, and more directly tied to winding down at night. Headspace, meanwhile, is better suited to people who want meditation to become part of their daytime routine as well as their nighttime routine. If meditation depth is the deciding factor for you, Headspace is probably the stronger pick. If meditation is something you want available inside a larger sleep-focused environment, BetterSleep strikes a better balance for most users looking primarily to improve sleep. Pricing — What You Actually Pay in 2026 Pricing matters more with sleep apps than people sometimes admit. As of May 2026, Headspace costs $12.99/month or $69.99/year, with discounted student pricing available. BetterSleep costs approximately $9.99/month or $59.99/year, making it slightly cheaper annually for standard users. BetterSleep also periodically offers a lifetime purchase around the $249 range, which changes the long-term math significantly for people who know they’ll use sleep audio every night. Headspace doesn’t currently offer an equivalent lifetime plan. Headspace’s free tier functions more like a limited preview of the platform. BetterSleep’s free version is more usable for casual nightly listening, especially if your main interest is ambient sound or basic sleep audio. Sleep apps are unusually personal. An app that works perfectly for one person may do almost nothing for someone else. If you mainly want a structured meditation platform with sleep benefits included, Headspace’s pricing makes sense relative to its course library and guided content depth. If your primary use case is nightly sleep support — soundscapes, sleep stories, bedtime routines, and environmental audio — BetterSleep generally delivers more sleep-specific functionality per dollar spent. Quick Pricing Comparison The Science — What Does the Research Actually Say? There is legitimate evidence that mindfulness practices, relaxation techniques, and digital sleep programs can improve sleep quality for some people. But no mainstream sleep app should be viewed as a standalone medical treatment for serious chronic insomnia. Headspace currently has the stronger direct clinical evidence. A 2025 randomized controlled trial involving Headspace’s “Finding Your Best Sleep” program reported a 29% reduction in self-reported insomnia symptoms over 18 days, along with improvements in sleep quality and daytime functioning. Earlier research has also linked mindfulness-based app use with improvements in sleep duration, sleep quality, and daytime tiredness in working adults. BetterSleep is approaching the problem from a different angle. The app focuses more on environmental audio, relaxation, nighttime routines, and personalized sound environments than structured therapeutic programs. There is evidence that relaxing audio, sound masking, and consistent bedtime routines can help support sleep quality and make it easier for some people to fall asleep, particularly when environmental noise or nighttime overstimulation is part of the problem. Some features inside BetterSleep — particularly binaural beats and solfeggio frequencies — are still being studied, and the evidence around them is less definitive. But the broader idea behind the app’s sleep-first approach is not especially controversial: a calmer, more consistent nighttime environment helps many people sleep better. The best sleep app usually isn’t the one with the strongest clinical paper attached to it. It’s the one you’ll consistently use on a stressful Tuesday night when your brain refuses to slow down. Who Should Choose Which? Choose BetterSleep if: you mainly struggle with falling asleep,

background noise or environmental sound matters to you,

you like customizing audio,

you want sleep stories and soundscapes first,

or you want a sleep-focused app that also includes meditation tools. Choose Headspace if: your sleep problems are closely tied to stress or anxious thinking,

you want a structured meditation practice,

you prefer guided programs over customization,

or you want stronger mindfulness and CBT-I-style content inside the app. For most users, choosing one and committing to it consistently for several weeks is more effective than constantly switching between platforms looking for a perfect solution. Conclusion Headspace and BetterSleep are both strong apps, but they’re designed around different priorities. Headspace is still the stronger meditation platform overall. Its structured courses, mindfulness framework, and CBT-I-informed sleep program give it more depth for users focused on stress reduction and long-term meditation practice. BetterSleep is more purpose-built for sleep support. Its sound mixer, customizable audio environment, sleep stories, bedtime tools, and lower annual pricing make it a better fit for many users whose primary goal is simply falling asleep faster and building more consistent nighttime routines — especially if factors like environmental noise or inconsistent sleep habits tend to interfere with sleep quality. If you want meditation first and sleep second, choose Headspace. If you want sleep first and meditation second, BetterSleep is probably the better fit. FAQ Is Headspace or BetterSleep better for sleep? Both apps can improve sleep, but they approach the problem differently. Headspace focuses more heavily on mindfulness, meditation, and CBT-I-informed sleep support, while BetterSleep centers the experience around customizable soundscapes, bedtime audio, sleep stories, and nightly routines. If stress and racing thoughts are the main issue, Headspace may be the stronger option. If your focus is falling asleep faster or building a more personalized nighttime environment, BetterSleep generally feels more sleep-focused overall. How much does each app cost in 2026? As of May 2026, Headspace costs $12.99/month or $69.99/year, with discounted student pricing available. BetterSleep costs about $9.99/month or $59.99/year and periodically offers a lifetime purchase option around $249. BetterSleep is slightly cheaper annually and offers more long-term pricing flexibility for people who know they’ll be using the app long term. Does Headspace have sleep tracking? Not really. Headspace tracks meditation activity and mindfulness progress, but it does not function as a dedicated sleep tracking app. BetterSleep includes microphone-based sleep tracking and snore detection designed to provide general nightly insights and habit awareness. Users looking for highly detailed biometric sleep-stage analysis will still get more accurate data from wearable devices like Apple Watch, Fitbit, or Oura. Can I use both Headspace and BetterSleep together? Yes. Headspace works well as a daytime meditation and mindfulness platform, while BetterSleep is often used more heavily at night for soundscapes, sleep stories, and bedtime audio. The downside is cost. Maintaining both subscriptions can become expensive over time, which is why many users eventually settle on the app that best matches their primary sleep or relaxation needs. Which app has better sleep stories? BetterSleep offers a larger and more varied library overall, with multiple narration styles and a wider range of story types. Headspace’s Sleepcasts tend to feel more polished and tightly produced, with especially strong ambient sound design. If you value variety and customization, BetterSleep has the edge here. If you prefer a more curated and guided listening experience, Headspace may appeal more.

data.title: Personalized AI Therapy: How Adaptive Technologies Are Changing Mental Healthcare (2026)
data.ai_summary: This article surveys the landscape of AI-driven personalized therapy in mental healthcare, explaining three levels of personalization (static, dynamic, and just-in-time adaptive interventions), and notes that while commercial apps like Woebot, Wysa, Youper, Headspace, and Calm have incorporated adaptive features, none yet achieves true just-in-time adaptive intervention levels. The piece identifies machine learning-based treatment matching as a promising frontier, though clinical deployment remains in early stages, while raising concerns about the privacy risks inherent in collecting sensitive mental health data for personalization purposes.
data.full_text:
Personalized AI Therapy: How Adaptive Technologies Are Changing Mental Healthcare

Traditional mental health treatment applies population-level evidence to individual cases: guidelines developed from group studies are used to inform care for specific people. This works reasonably well on average but imperfectly for any given individual. Personalized medicine — tailoring treatment to the individual's biology, history, and real-time state — has transformed oncology and other medical fields. AI-driven personalization is beginning to do the same for mental health care.

What Personalized AI Therapy Means

Personalized AI therapy refers to digital mental health interventions that adapt their content, timing, intensity, and approach based on data about the specific user — rather than delivering the same standardized program to everyone. This adaptation can occur at multiple levels:

Static personalization: Tailoring content to stated preferences, history, and symptom profile at intake. An app that asks about your key concerns and delivers relevant content accordingly is using static personalization.

Dynamic personalization: Adapting content in real time based on ongoing user behavior and responses. If a user consistently skips breathing exercises but engages with journaling prompts, a dynamically personalized system shifts toward more journaling content.

Just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs): Perhaps the most sophisticated approach — delivering the right intervention at the right moment, based on real-time sensor data. If wearable data suggests elevated physiological stress, the system delivers a brief stress reduction exercise at that moment. This is the frontier of personalized mental health technology.

The Science Behind Adaptive Interventions

The just-in-time adaptive intervention model was conceptualized by researchers including Susan Murphy at Harvard, and developed through the field of "micro-randomized trials" — experimental designs that randomize treatment decisions at the moment level rather than the person level. This allows researchers to identify which interventions work for which people under which conditions.

Early work with JITAIs has shown promise for:

Alcohol use disorder (HeartSteps and related programs)

Smoking cessation

Physical activity promotion

Depression and anxiety management

The research is still developing — most JITAI studies are small and short-term — but the theoretical framework is sound and the early signals are encouraging.

Machine Learning and Treatment Matching

One of the most exciting applications of AI in personalized mental health care is treatment matching: using algorithms to predict which treatment approach will work best for a specific person.

Current treatment selection is largely trial-and-error. First-line treatments for depression (SSRIs, CBT) work for about half of patients. For those who don't respond, the next step is trying something else. This iterative process can take years and involves significant suffering.

Machine learning approaches attempt to identify biomarkers — biological, psychological, and behavioral patterns — that predict treatment response. Research programs including the ISPOT-D study (which identified brain imaging patterns predicting differential response to SSRIs vs. CBT) and the PrediCT project (using language patterns to predict SSRI response) suggest this is achievable in principle.

Clinical deployment of treatment-matching algorithms is still in early stages, but several systems are moving toward implementation:

Predictive algorithms to guide antidepressant selection based on pharmacogenomic data

Machine learning models predicting therapy dropout, allowing preventive intervention

Natural language processing of therapy session transcripts to identify therapists whose approach best matches specific client presentations

Personalization in Current Commercial Apps

Commercial mental health apps have incorporated personalization features to varying degrees:

Woebot: One of the more sophisticated chatbot-based systems. Uses CBT principles delivered through a conversational AI that adapts its approach based on user responses and mood tracking data.

Wysa: An AI-powered emotional support chatbot that tracks mood patterns and tailors tool recommendations accordingly.

Youper: Combines AI-powered conversations with mood tracking to personalize emotional regulation support.

Headspace and Calm: Have both incorporated adaptive features that recommend content based on usage history, stated preferences, and reported outcomes.

None of these systems represents true JITAI-level personalization, but they represent meaningful steps beyond static programs.

What Personalization Can and Cannot Achieve

What it can do:

Increase engagement by delivering more relevant content

Reduce friction by removing interventions users consistently skip

Potentially improve outcomes by matching intervention type to individual response patterns

Provide support at the most relevant moments through just-in-time delivery

What it cannot do:

Replace the personalization inherent in a strong therapeutic relationship — where a skilled clinician interprets subtle cues, responds to unexpressed needs, and adjusts in real time with genuine understanding

Handle the complexity of severe or treatment-resistant conditions where personalization requires clinical expertise

Guarantee privacy when the data powering personalization may be sensitive and commercially valuable

Eliminate the engagement decay problem — personalization helps but doesn't fully solve the issue of users stopping app use over time

The Privacy Challenge

Personalized AI therapy requires rich individual data. The more personalized the system, the more data it collects: mood history, physiological signals, behavioral patterns, content of written and spoken disclosures. This data is deeply sensitive.

The privacy practices of commercial mental health technology companies have been criticized repeatedly for insufficient transparency, inadequate security, and commercial data sharing that users haven't meaningfully consented to. The more sophisticated the personalization, the more acute this concern.

Conclusion

Personalized AI therapy represents a genuinely exciting frontier in mental health technology. The prospect of interventions that arrive at the right moment, adapt to your individual response, and eventually predict which treatment will work best for you — not for the average patient, but for you specifically — is compelling and potentially transformative. The research foundations are real, even if clinical deployment lags behind the potential. The key challenge is ensuring that personalization serves users' wellbeing rather than commercial optimization — and that the data powering it is held with the care it deserves.

data.title: Foodsmart Adds Product and Commercial Chiefs as Medicaid Plans Search for Lower-Cost Care Models

data.full_text:
Foodsmart has expanded its executive leadership team with the appointments of Johnson Lieu as chief product officer and Jason Stenta as chief commercial officer as the company scales its nutrition-based healthcare platform amid growing payer demand for lower-cost chronic disease management solutions.

The hires come as Medicaid and Medicare organizations face mounting financial pressure tied to obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and rapidly rising utilization of GLP-1 medications. Foodsmart is positioning itself within a growing healthcare category that combines nutrition therapy, food benefits management, and behavioral support into payer-backed care infrastructure aimed at reducing long-term medical spending.

CEO Kurt Knight said the company’s strategy extends beyond traditional dietitian referrals and telehealth nutrition services.

“Foodcare combines Medical Nutrition Therapy delivered by our RD network with Food Benefits Management that ensures every dollar is clinically justified and guides members toward self-sufficiency,” Knight said.

The executive additions underscore Foodsmart’s broader effort to establish “foodcare” as a scalable clinical and reimbursement category within healthcare delivery, particularly as insurers increasingly integrate social determinants of health and value-based care economics into population health strategies.

Lieu joins Foodsmart from Headspace, where he served as senior vice president of product and interim chief product officer following the company’s merger with telehealth provider Ginger. His background also includes senior product leadership roles at Spotify and Electronic Arts, experience that may prove increasingly relevant as healthcare companies focus more heavily on patient engagement, long-term adherence, and consumer-style digital experiences.

At Foodsmart, Lieu will oversee product strategy, AI development, and platform expansion efforts focused on Medicaid and Medicare populations.

“What drew me to Foodsmart is the rare combination of a meaningful mission, ambitious trajectory, and genuinely passionate talent,” Lieu said.

Stenta brings more than two decades of healthcare and payer commercialization experience, most recently serving as chief commercial officer at Walgreens U.S. Healthcare. His prior leadership roles at Optum, CVS Health, and Change Healthcare centered on payer partnerships, value-based care models, and healthcare economics.

His appointment reflects growing pressure on nutrition and food-as-medicine companies to demonstrate measurable financial returns for health plans and government-funded healthcare programs increasingly scrutinizing cost-containment strategies.

Foodsmart paired the leadership announcement with new operational data intended to reinforce the economic case for its model.

The company said its Food Benefits Management program reduced unvetted food-benefit spending by 50% to 75% while generating net savings of $54 per member per month among individuals receiving medical nutrition therapy and medically tailored food support.

Foodsmart also reported that members using GLP-1 therapies alongside concurrent nutrition counseling saved an additional $168 per member per month compared with matched patients using GLP-1 drugs alone.

Those figures are likely intended to resonate with Medicaid organizations and other healthcare payers now grappling with the long-term budget implications of expanding obesity and diabetes drug utilization.

The company’s broader strategy reflects a larger shift underway across healthcare markets, where nutrition access, behavioral support, and food benefits are increasingly being treated as clinical infrastructure rather than supplemental wellness services.

Foodsmart currently serves more than 3 million members through partnerships with health plans, healthcare providers, and employers. Its platform integrates registered dietitian care, meal planning, food-access programs, and benefits management into a unified care model designed to address diet-related chronic conditions at scale.

The executive additions complete what Foodsmart described as a fully built-out leadership team spanning product, technology, clinical operations, commercial strategy, customer experience, and finance as the company expands adoption across government and commercial healthcare markets.

His focus: translating Foodsmart's clinical evidence and deep member understanding into products that drive adoption and impact at scale. I've spent my career building products at the intersection of technology and human need, and I've learned that the most impactful ones come from truly understanding what people need and committing to serve them well. Foodsmart's foodcare model—integrating registered dietitian care, personalized meal planning, and food access into healthcare—is exactly the kind of solution I want to dedicate my energy to. I'm excited to translate our clinical evidence and member insights into a product that scales our impact nationwide." Jason Stenta, Chief Commercial Officer Jason Stenta brings more than 20 years of healthcare commercial experience, most recently serving as Chief Commercial Officer at Walgreens U.S. Healthcare. Throughout his career, he has held growth-focused leadership roles at Optum, Change Healthcare, and CVS Health, where he has built and scaled commercial teams, structured multi-year value-based partnerships with health plans, and driven growth across Government and Commercial markets. His deep expertise in healthcare economics, payer relationships, and value-based care arrangements positions him well to lead Foodsmart's commercial expansion. At Foodsmart, Jason will lead the sales organization and government affairs, working to expand partnerships with health plans and providers. His focus: helping payers understand and operationalize foodcare at scale, and ensuring Foodsmart's go-to-market strategy reflects the clinical evidence and economic value it's proven. Said Jason Stenta: "Foodsmart's clinical rigor and demonstrated improvements in health outcomes and total cost of care position us to be the partner of choice for payers and providers across the country. We're establishing foodcare as a distinct clinical category—one that combines registered dietitian care, food access, and behavior change into a replicable benefit model. With our RD network, patient engagement programs, food partnerships, and holistic Food Benefit Management approach, we're proving that foodcare works at scale. I'm thrilled to be joining Foodsmart's leadership team during this transformational time." Proven ROI Across Key Medicaid Cost Drivers These hires come as Foodsmart releases new clinical data demonstrating the foodcare model's impact on two of Medicaid's most pressing cost challenges: the need for clinically-governed food benefit management and escalating GLP-1 pharmacy spend. Food Benefits Management: Clinical Governance Over Unvetted Spend

Across Medicaid populations, unvetted food benefit spend represents significant audit exposure and waste, with benefits approved on member or vendor self-attestation rather than clinical need. Foodsmart's Food Benefits Management program applies RD-gated authorization, risk stratification, and a guided graduation path to member independence. Foodsmart RDs facilitate every member's transition from intensive food support toward sustainable behavior change—proven to graduate 92% of members and deliver meaningful total medical cost savings. Results show a 50-75% reduction in unvetted food spend and $54 PMPM in net savings across members receiving medical nutrition therapy and medically tailored food. GLP-1 + Medical Nutrition Therapy: Amplifying Outcomes, Offsetting Costs

For GLP-1 therapy, now the fastest-growing category in Medicaid pharmacy spending, members who received concurrent medical nutrition therapy saved $168 per member per month more than matched members on GLP-1s alone, translating to approximately $2,016 in annual net savings per member. For a 5,000-member plan on GLP-1 therapy, this represents roughly $10 million in annual net savings while reducing chronic disease cost trajectory over the 3–5 year horizon. Foodsmart's RD-led approach addresses the clinical gap GLP-1 medications alone cannot solve: behavioral change, food access, and sustained adherence. Johnson and Jason join a fully built-out executive team that now spans product, technology, clinical, commercial, customer experience, and finance. Together, they can help Foodsmart's customers, Medicaid, Medicare, and commercial plans, replicate outcomes like these at scale—operationalizing the foodcare model across food benefit management, high-risk populations, and the full spectrum of diet-related chronic disease. Headspace survey finds nine in 10 U.S. workers are experiencing mental or cognitive strain on the job; for more than a third, it’s gotten worse over the past year The company’s eighth annual report highlights an emerging chronic strain crisis, pointing to unclear company priorities, job security, and AI as top driving forces

Headspace 2026 Workforce State of Mind Report

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Headspace, the leading mental health companion for everyday support, today released its eighth annual Workforce State of Mind report, with data pointing to an emerging chronic strain crisis across the workforce stemming from the slow, relentless accumulation of mental and cognitive pressure that never fully powers down. With 92% of workers experiencing strain, these pressures have quietly intensified. About 37% of workers say that strain has increased in the past 12 months. We can’t keep waiting until people are already burned out to act. The ones that tackle this gap earlier will have teams that can more confidently keep pace and better support their people. Share Behind the crisis is a workforce navigating too much change, too fast. Unclear company priorities, job insecurity, and constant organizational shifts have emerged as the top sources of strain, with AI adoption as the underpinning force of change fatigue. About 70% of employees say their organization has adopted new AI technologies, making it the single most common form of organizational change workers have experienced over the past year. “Mental and cognitive strain are locked in a loop. You can't think straight when you're stressed, and you can't de-stress when your mind won't stop. AI is pouring fuel on that fire. We're seeing it at every level with workers running on empty at the exact moment they're being asked to do the hardest thinking of their careers,” said Lisa Mulrooney Gross, chief people officer at Headspace. “We can’t keep waiting until people are already burned out to act. The ones that tackle this gap earlier will have teams that can more confidently keep pace and better support their people.” Key findings from the report: AI is raising the bar for productivity at work and simultaneously eroding the very cognitive skills workers need most, with 76% unable to sleep and nearly half saying strain has compromised their judgment when using AI. Over 70% of workers report mental or cognitive strain has negatively affected their sleep (76%), ability to focus (73%), and productivity at work (70%).

44% say mental or cognitive strain has affected their ability to apply good judgment when using AI and new technologies. Unclear priorities, job insecurity, and constant change are taking the biggest toll; 58% of workers are facing it without any resilience training. The top drivers of strain are unclear priorities (41%), job insecurity (37%), the pace of organizational change (29%), context-switching (26%), and use of new technologies including AI (24%).

Among workers navigating organizational change, 51% have emotionally checked out, and 45% have felt resentful toward leadership.

58% of workers say they haven’t had a single hour of resilience, stress management, emotional intelligence, change management, or other cognitive skill training in the past year.

44% of people managers believe they’ve equipped individual contributors with the resilience skills to handle constant change, but only 23% of individual contributors agree. The data show a consistent and troubling gender gap in workforce wellbeing. Women are carrying more strain, and receiving less; only 27% say their organization is meeting their mental health needs. 73% of women say mental or cognitive strain have hurt their productivity vs. 67% of men.

Women report worse sleep quality (83% vs. 70%), inability to focus (80% vs. 67%), and disengagement at work (69% vs. 59%).

Only 27% say their organization is meeting their mental health needs vs. 34% of men. In addition to a comprehensive overview of the survey data, Headspace’s 2026 Workforce State of Mind report offers a roadmap for organizations on what to do next by supporting employees where they are, before challenges escalate. Alongside the data, the report includes a resilience strategy guide and free mental health resources from Headspace’s Mindfulness at Work collection. To download the report, visit https://hubs.li/Q04gtpDf0. Methodology Headspace commissioned YouGov to conduct a survey among 724 total U.S. workers aged 25 to 69, employed full-time at companies with more than 1,000 employees. Data was collected between April 3rd to 16th, 2026 and has a margin of error of ± 3.6% at the 95% level of confidence. Of the total, 505 are employees (individual contributors) and 219 are employers (people leaders). The data are not weighted. About Headspace Headspace is the leading everyday mental health companion, helping people care for their minds anytime, anywhere. Our all-in-one app delivers personalized support — from AI-powered guidance to meditation and mindfulness, coaching, and therapy — all designed to fit seamlessly into daily life. We are partnered with over 4,000 employers, health plans, and organizations to extend mental health care to their communities with a population health-led approach, offering additional services including psychiatry, EAP, care navigation, and work-life resources. Our team is made up of world-class clinicians, Emmy Award-winning storytellers, and leading AI technologists, working together to help millions around the globe build resilience and feel better. In a busy, complicated world, Headspace is here to remind you: your mind matters. Learn more at headspace.com.
